records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
Input size: A parameter for resource analysis, such as record count n.
Cost model: Explicitly chosen operations and their relative costs, rather than CPU frequency.
O: An asymptotic upper bound up to a constant factor beyond some n.
Ω: An asymptotic lower bound for the same definition of cost.
Θ: Matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds.
Worst case: The maximum cost over valid inputs of a fixed size.
Amortization: A bound on a sequence of operations, rather than a random average input.
Auxiliary space: Working storage beyond the agreed input and output representation.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
Separate a correct result, termination and the cost of processing a growing input.
Define input size and the counted operation.
Derive an exact sum for a nested loop.
Distinguish O, Ω and Θ on concrete functions.
Justify time and auxiliary space separately.
Check a counter on empty input and the upper boundary.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
Input size belongs to the model
For sorting, n usually counts records; for text it may count characters or bytes; a matrix needs two dimensions. Define it before writing O(n). A numeric value and its representation length are different sizes: a loop up to m can execute m steps although a binary representation of m needs roughly log₂m bits.
Also define the cost of a comparison. Here bounded integers are compared and one comparison counts as one operation. Comparing long strings can inspect several bytes, while reading a file includes I/O. A comparison-count estimate remains useful, but cannot silently be renamed the entire program’s running time.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
An exact counter and a cost function
Let the selected operation be a counter increment in the body. One loop from 0 through n−1 performs it n times. If an inner loop visits j from i+1 through n−1, the total is (n−1)+(n−2)+…+0=n(n−1)/2. At n=4 there are six pairs; at n=0 there are none. Enumerate the pairs and compare them with a trace.
Condition checks, index increments and output have costs too, but this counter does not include them. The formula is exact for the explicitly selected operation. Changing the model changes coefficients and lower-order terms. Do not tune the counter to produce a preferred curve: specify what will be counted first.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
O, Ω and Θ without verbal shortcuts
For nonnegative functions, O(g(n)) is an upper bound: some constant c>0 and threshold n₀ make T(n)≤c·g(n) for all later n. Ω gives a lower bound using the reverse inequality. Θ means both bounds hold at the same growth order. Thus T(n)=n(n−1)/2 is Θ(n²), although it also belongs to O(n³).
O does not mean “worst case”, nor does Ω mean “best case”. First choose a function, such as the maximum comparisons over all inputs of length n; then bound it with O or Θ. Asymptotics describes a family of sizes, so finite runs up to n=128 do not prove it. The implementation has a finite domain; the growth argument uses an explicitly stated abstract model.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
Best, average, worst and amortized cost
Linear search can find the target immediately, scan the entire collection or fail to find it. Best and worst cases answer different questions. An average requires a probability model of inputs: one arbitrary seed is not an average case. A user-facing service also needs an acceptable maximum, particularly when another person chooses the input.
An amortized bound describes a sequence of operations, not a random input distribution. A vector append can occasionally reallocate the whole buffer: one append is expensive, while a series spreads that cost across its operations. “Usually” conceals the distinction unless the model is named. State whether your report estimates one query, a full sequence or index construction.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
An invariant explains the state
A loop invariant is a statement true before each iteration. For a running sum it could be “sum equals the sum of the first i items”. Prove initialization, preservation by one step and the conclusion at termination. Merely having a variable i proves nothing; connect it to the processed input and the observable result.
For pair enumeration, the outer invariant says all pairs whose first index is below i have been counted exactly once. An inner step adds one new pair (i,j). The condition j>i excludes the diagonal and mirrored duplicates. This explains both the counter’s correctness and its cost, but write those conclusions separately.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
Termination, bounds and safe arithmetic
A finite loop needs a termination variant: a nonnegative integer that decreases, such as n−i. Check it around continue and any counter updates inside the body. A search can decrease interval length. A wrong boundary update can leave the length unchanged and cause an otherwise correct comparison to repeat forever.
The lab accepts n=0…128, bounding pair count by 8128. Validate the range before looping; long long provides explicit headroom. The formula n·(n−1)/2 does not prevent overflow for arbitrary n. Unsigned n−1 at zero also needs care: prove its precondition or choose a loop form safe for an empty collection.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
Memory and preparation belong to the decision
Distinguish storage for input from auxiliary algorithm storage. Sorting a copy uses another array even if the sorting algorithm itself is in-place. Recursion stores call state; a map uses nodes or buckets. O(1) auxiliary space does not mean zero bytes, and exact sizes depend on types, libraries and architecture.
Building a sorted index can pay off across many queries yet be wasteful for one search. Compare preparation plus q queries. Models n·q for repeated scans and n log n + q log n for an index help formulate a hypothesis. They omit constants and do not replace measuring a particular implementation on appropriate data.

records.title: Complexity, invariants and correctness
records.text:
From a model to an auditable report
A report should include the contract, definition of n, selected operation, exact formula or justified bounds and raw observations. Derive expectations before each run. If counts disagree, seek a minimal counterexample: empty, singleton or two-item input. Revising the expectation after seeing output destroys the check’s independence.
Nexus may prepare a compiler on first use, and UI/browser work affects latency. Those costs are not your algorithm’s comparison count. Use counters now; repeated timing methodology comes later in the module. The next lesson applies invariants and models to sorting and shows why “ascending” alone is not a complete sorting contract.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Definiteness: The intended action of each step is unambiguous.
Invariant: A property that remains true across specified state transitions.
Postcondition: A property that must hold when the algorithm finishes.
Termination measure: A well-founded quantity that decreases as execution makes progress.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
An algorithm transforms input into a result through steps that a specified executor can follow without guessing.
State preconditions, postconditions and algorithm steps.
Distinguish definiteness, discrete steps, generality and termination.
Trace the program state after each step.
Describe how invariants and decreasing measures support correctness reasoning.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Turn an informal task into precise steps
An instruction such as 'repeat until the number is small' leaves 'small' undefined. An algorithm needs an explicit condition, state update and result.
We can state a Euclidean step precisely: while b is not zero, replace (a,b) by (b,a modulo b). With a suitable input domain, a programmer can implement and test the process.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Definiteness and discreteness
Discreteness means reasoning about a computation as a sequence of individual steps. Definiteness means the executor can identify the intended operation at each step.
Different programming languages may implement the same algorithm. Precise transitions let us trace intermediate states and compare implementations.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Termination, the input domain and generality
A terminating algorithm must finish for every input in its stated domain. A condition such as n >= 0 matters: a loop designed for positive counts may misbehave outside that domain.
Generality means solving a class of related instances, not a single hard-coded example. A sound addition algorithm should work for multiple valid pairs.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Correctness requires more than stopping
A program may halt quickly and still produce the wrong result. We must establish both a terminating process and a postcondition satisfied by its output.
In Euclid's algorithm, replacing (a,b) with (b,a mod b) preserves the greatest common divisor; when b becomes zero, a is the answer. This illustrates invariant-based reasoning.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Identify an exit condition before coding the loop
A nonnegative quantity that strictly decreases often explains termination. But you must check that each transition actually reduces the quantity under the preconditions.
Changing a loop requires revisiting its invariant and exit condition. Forgetting to update a counter can turn a correct finite loop into an infinite one.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Contract and postcondition
For 125 seconds, the result is 2 minutes and 5 seconds: 125 = 60·2 + 5. Zero produces 0 and 0. The general postcondition is seconds = 60·minutes + remainder with 0 ≤ remainder < 60. Integer / gives the quotient and % the remainder. Once nonnegative input has been checked, these operations match ordinary division.

records.title: Algorithms: precision, termination and correctness
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
Integer inputs must fit the Code Studio int type. Failed extraction (text instead of a number or end of input) produces invalid; no further calculation is performed.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
Pseudocode: A readable description of algorithmic steps without a single language's concrete syntax.
Decision table: A table pairing relevant conditions with their expected actions.
Flowchart: A diagram of actions and branches linked by directed connections.
Trace: A record of the evolving program state through execution steps.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
A single algorithm can be expressed in different forms. Each form exposes a different type of mistake or assumption.
Translate requirements into a decision table and pseudocode.
Check that a flowchart expresses the same conditions as the algorithm.
Distinguish abstract steps from executable C++.
Trace all branches using explicit inputs.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
Different representations expose different concerns
Consider classifying an integer as negative, zero or positive. In natural language it seems obvious, but we might forget the zero case when implementing it.
A decision table enumerates all cases, pseudocode shows the evaluation order, a flowchart makes branches visible and C++ implements the transitions.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
Decision tables test completeness
Write the conditions x<0, x==0 and x>0, each with one expected action. This reveals omitted or overlapping cases before code is written.
If a valid input does not belong to any row, the requirement is incomplete. For a sign classifier, the zero row is essential.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
Pseudocode makes the sequence explicit
A clear version reads: IF x<0 print negative; ELSE IF x==0 print zero; ELSE print positive. The logic can be reviewed by someone who does not yet know iostream.
Pseudocode conventions vary. Always state inputs, outputs and nesting unambiguously; pseudocode itself is not executable C++.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
Flowcharts visualize control flow
An oval commonly denotes start/end, a rectangle an action, and a diamond a condition. Arrows indicate the next step, with true/false paths labeled.
A flowchart is only useful if a reader can follow every input to the correct output. Unlabeled branches or arrows are a source of confusion.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
Code is a concrete implementation
Compare each pseudocode condition with the corresponding C++ branch. The remainder operator % is commonly used to test parity through x%2==0.
Check x=-5, x=0 and x=7. Equal observed results across these examples support consistency, though finite tests do not prove all possible cases.

records.title: Representing algorithms: decision tables, pseudocode, flowcharts and code
records.text:
From the decision table to code
The sign table has three rows: x<0 → negative; x=0 → zero; x>0 → positive. They are mutually exclusive and cover the allowed integers. C++ uses == for equality and = for assignment. An if / else if / else chain selects one branch. Three independent if statements need a separate condition audit and are not always equivalent.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Integer quotient: The result of integer / with the fractional part discarded toward zero.
Remainder: For valid integer division, related to the quotient by a = (a / b) * b + a % b.
Compound assignment: An operation such as stock += 4 that updates the left object using its previous value.
Intermediate range: A bound on each expression value before the final result is stored.
Signed overflow: A signed arithmetic result outside its representable range; it must not be executed as a normal test.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Check integer division, express state changes concisely, and calculate block counts without overflow.
Calculate / and % for positive and negative integers.
Distinguish assignment from compound +=, −=, *=, /=, %=.
Choose a wide type before the first potentially overflowing multiplication.
Round a nonnegative block count upward with proven bounds.
Distinguish invalid division from a legitimate boundary test.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Session 1. Integer division has its own contract
For integers, 7 / 3 is 2. −7 / 3 is −2: the fraction is discarded toward zero rather than rounded down to −3. −7 % 3 is −1 because −7 = (−2) × 3 + (−1). A nonzero remainder has the dividend’s sign, not necessarily the divisor’s.
Check 7 / −3 and −7 / −3 with the same identity. This is not the always-nonnegative mathematical modulo used in some tasks. Do not assume % produces an index in 0…b−1 for negative inputs. Here we explain the result; range normalization belongs to a later concrete task.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Exclude invalid operations before computing
For integers a zero divisor is invalid for both / and %. Another dangerous boundary is the minimum signed value divided by −1 when the quotient is unrepresentable. A successful build does not make these runtime operations valid. We do not execute them for an error screenshot.
The laboratory scaffold checks invalid bounds before dividing. || means or: if any rejection condition is true, it prints invalid and return 0 ends processing. This repeats the protective scaffold from Module 1 rather than requiring new independent branching design.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Read compound assignment as a state change
For a simple int stock, stock += 4; adds 4, stock -= 3; subtracts 3, and stock *= 2; doubles it. The sequence is 10 → 14 → 11 → 22. /= and %= replace the value with the quotient and remainder. Division and range restrictions still apply.
For a simple name, x += y updates x with the sum. Do not generalize this to a blind textual rewrite of complex left expressions: compound assignment evaluates its left operand once. We use ordinary names only, without arrays, pointers, or effectful functions.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Session 2. A wide destination cannot widen the past
Let width and height be ints equal to 50000. In long long area = width * height;, the product is evaluated as int when both operands remain int. On a target with 32-bit int, 2500000000 does not fit. The wider area destination cannot help. We discuss this unsafe form without executing it.
In the safe example 1LL is a long long literal with value 1. 1LL * width * height starts multiplication in a wide integer type. These small nonnegative operands convert safely. Another solution is to declare both operands long long initially. General promotions and conversions follow next; the essential point is widening before the dangerous step.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
How many whole blocks are needed?
With bytes=1001 and blockBytes=1000 the quotient is 1 and remainder 1: one full block, but two are needed for storage. For bytes ≥ 0 and blockBytes > 0, (bytes + blockBytes - 1) / blockBytes rounds upward. Zero volume needs zero blocks and an exact multiple needs no extra block.
The formula is not automatically safe near a type maximum: the addition can overflow. We bound bytes to 1000000000000 and blockBytes to 4096, so the numerator is at most 1000000004095 and fits long long. Bounds are checked first. A different contract requires a new proof or another formula.

records.title: Arithmetic and assignment: quotient, remainder, and safe intermediates
records.text:
Boundary cases beat random runs
For a block size of 1000, test volumes 0, 999, 1000, and 1001. They distinguish empty volume, remainder, an exact multiple, and the next block. Also test blockBytes=0: expect invalid without executing division.
Record the maximum intermediate bound as well as output. A sanitizer helps find defects in tests, but a few clean runs do not replace reasoning over the stated range. The diagram below traces only the valid example −7 / 3.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Key: A value used to determine record identity.
map: An ordered collection of unique keys and mapped values.
set: An ordered collection of unique keys without a separate mapped value.
unordered_map: A hash container with unique keys and unspecified traversal order.
Collision: Distinct keys sharing a hash, resolved using equivalence checks.
find: Lookup returning an iterator or end without inserting a key.
operator[]: Access to a mapped value that may insert a missing key.
rehash: Rebuilding buckets, invalidating iterators but not references to retained elements.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Distinguish ordering, unique keys, average hash cost and access side effects.
Choose set, map or unordered_map by contract.
Look up without hidden insertion.
Explain collisions and key equivalence.
Produce a deterministic report.
Distinguish average and worst-case complexity.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Keys, mapped values and uniqueness
A set stores keys; a map associates each key with a mapped value. In a frequency index, the word is the key and its occurrence count is the value. Repetition updates the count rather than adding a distinct key. Record-ID uniqueness is a separate domain rule: equal amounts may be allowed while duplicate IDs are not.
A map element resembles a pair: first is the key and second the mapped value. const auto& entry reads without copying; const auto& [word,count] names the parts through a structured binding. Do not mutate a map key in place because it would break lookup organization. Changing a key needs an explicit erase/insert design or another documented operation.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Ordered map and set
std::map and std::set keep keys under their comparator’s order. Lookup, insertion and erasure have logarithmic guarantees under their contracts. Balanced trees are common implementations, but the public interface does not require knowing a particular balancing scheme. Ordered traversal is useful when the report actually needs it.
Ordered-container uniqueness uses comparator equivalence: neither a precedes b nor b precedes a. This need not equal an arbitrary user-defined operator==. Our integers and ASCII strings use compatible ordinary ordering. Do not make lookup case-insensitive while insertion follows another order.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Unordered containers: hash and equality
unordered_map and unordered_set use hashing to organize lookup and equality to distinguish keys. Different keys can share a hash: a collision does not permit dropping one record. Many operations have constant-like average cost in element count under appropriate conditions; their worst case can be linear.
Equivalent keys must have equal hashes, and the chosen rules must stay consistent. Hashing and comparing strings inspect content, so O(1) in key count does not mean independence from string length. The lab bounds ASCII keys to twelve bytes, keeping input and comparison assumptions explicit.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
A read must not silently insert
counts[word] inserts a missing key with a value-initialized mapped value. For int with the standard allocator that is zero, making ++counts[word] useful for counting. But counts["missing"]==0 mutates the container even though it looks like a read. Use find and compare with end when asking whether a key exists, preserving map size.
end must not be dereferenced here either. Check the result before reading second. at can report absence with an exception; this runtime is not the EH teaching environment, so the lab uses explicit find. Distinguish a missing key from an existing mapped zero, which can represent a different domain state.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Invalidation is container-specific
Do not transfer vector rules to unordered_map without checking its contract. Rehash reorganizes buckets and invalidates iterators, while references and pointers to surviving elements remain valid under that operation’s rules. Erasure invalidates access to the erased item. reserve can rehash, so an earlier iterator is not automatically safe afterward.
Before iterating while inserting, determine whether rehash can occur; collecting changes separately is often simpler. A user catalogue can keep stable IDs and repeat find instead of storing iterators long-term. Valid iterators alone do not prevent logically stale data: an index must match the current dataset version.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Collisions and a testing scaffold
The supplied SameHash returns zero for every int, forcing collisions while equality still distinguishes keys. operator()(int) const makes its object callable so the container can obtain a hash value. Reading this scaffold is sufficient here; designing generic hash libraries belongs to a later module.
Check insertion, lookup of every key and erasure of one key. The experiment demonstrates collision correctness; it neither measures production performance nor makes the intentionally poor hash appropriate. A container hash is not a cryptographic primitive or a promise against adversarial input.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Deterministic reports and catalogue reconciliation
Do not expect stable unordered traversal across libraries, runs or rehashing. For a report, copy pairs into a vector and sort by key, or use an ordered map. Storage, lookup and presentation can use different structures; that is an explicit architectural boundary, not merely duplication for prettier stdout.
The cumulative practicum compares catalogues over a union of keys. For each ID distinguish old-only, new-only and both; compare values in the last case. find does not manufacture the absent side. Validate both inputs before reporting, or a malformed second catalogue can falsely resemble mass deletion.

records.title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
records.text:
Choose by workload and check independently
List insertions, point queries, range queries and ordered reports in the workload. A small immutable dataset can favor a sorted vector over a tree or hash; frequent mutation changes the tradeoff. Include preparation, memory, key length and worst-case guarantees rather than relying on an O(1) slogan.
Test emptiness, repeated keys, different insertion orders, invalid words and duplicate IDs. Compare frequencies with an independent scan of the original list. Save an explicitly ordered report. Next, a reproducible data generator will show why a seed alone does not make a whole experiment portable.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
Terminator: the zero char marking the end of a C string.
string_view: a non-owning char sequence with a length.
UTF-8: encoding code points using variable-length byte sequences.
Code point: a numeric position in the Unicode code space.
Grapheme: a perceived text unit, sometimes containing multiple code points.
npos: a special no-position value returned by search.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
Distinguish std::string, C strings, and string_view, with an explicit ASCII and UTF-8 policy.
Explain: Character arrays and C strings
Trace: std::string owns a sequence
Justify: string_view does not own
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not retain string_view into a temporary string. Do not call isalpha with a potentially negative char.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
Character arrays and C strings
char word[4]{'c','a','t','\0'} is a C string with three letters and a null terminator. char letters[3]{'c','a','t'} is a three-char array, but not a C string. Passing it to a function that searches for \0 violates that function’s precondition.
The array size includes terminator storage; the text length before it does not. An embedded zero byte ends a C string before the buffer ends. Demonstrate the distinction with bounded valid examples, never by executing an unterminated read.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
std::string owns a sequence
std::string tracks its own char count and may contain embedded \0 data. size() counts chars, not visible letters. c_str() supplies a null-terminated compatibility buffer; do not retain its pointer across string mutation or owner destruction.
operator>> reads a whitespace-delimited token. getline reads a line without its terminating newline and retains internal spaces. Choose according to the format: a project name may contain spaces while a command code may be one ASCII token.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
ASCII and UTF-8
In UTF-8 one code point can occupy several bytes. Four Cyrillic letters commonly occupy eight bytes, while a perceived character may itself contain several code points. size() promises neither code-point nor grapheme count.
The lab classifies only ASCII A…Z, a…z, 0…9, and ordinary space. Other bytes count as other without modifying the original string. This is an explicit limited contract, not Unicode normalization or collation.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
string_view does not own
std::string_view from <string_view> holds a pointer and a length into another object’s text. It is convenient for read-only parameters but does not extend a std::string’s lifetime. A view’s substr creates another view; converting to std::string creates an owned copy.
A view need not end in \0. Do not pass view.data() to a C-string API without proving termination. Never return a view into a local string or mutate an owner in a way that may relocate its buffer while the view is in use.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
Search, emptiness, and byte classes
find returns a position or std::string::npos. Check the result and bounds before substr because the current runtime does not support exceptions. An empty line may be valid under the format; it differs from a failed getline with no line available.
For <cctype>, pass a value representable as unsigned char or EOF; a negative char is invalid. Direct unsigned-char comparisons against ASCII boundaries avoid locale-dependent classification here. An individual UTF-8 byte must not be edited as though it were a whole letter.

records.title: Strings: bytes, terminators, and safe views
records.text:
Text-interface tests
Test an empty line, spaces only, mixed letters and digits, internal spaces, and UTF-8. The lab limit is 200 bytes. Input must contain exactly one line; a second line, even empty, is extra data.
Preserve the original bytes and expected categories without claiming to count human-perceived characters. Next, a struct will group text, numbers, and status into one record without mixing their meanings.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Encapsulation: Controlling state through an interface that preserves domain meaning.
Public access: Members available to ordinary client code.
Private access: Language-restricted access without a promise of encrypted storage.
Const member function: A method that disallows ordinary mutation of the object through this.
Observer: An operation that reports state according to a contract.
Precondition: A condition required before a valid call.
Postcondition: A promise about result and state when a call finishes.
Domain atomicity: Completing a related update while preserving a joint invariant.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Design operations that prevent callers from violating related constraints.
Write transition tables for receive and ship.
Explain const Stock& in the example.
Test shipping nine after receiving eight.
Replace two interval setters with one operation.
Design a result with rejection reasons.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
An interface is a set of promises
Stock models a quantity between zero and one hundred. receive and ship are not merely ways to assign a field: they define valid transitions. Receiving cannot exceed capacity, and shipping cannot create a negative quantity. Before coding, describe the pre-call state, success condition, resulting state and behaviour on rejection.
Test the public interface as a client who cannot access a private field. A quantity() observer can establish a successful delivery and preservation after rejection. A test that bypasses access control becomes tied to implementation. It would obstruct a representation change even if the application's observable result remained unchanged.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Private and public
class and struct differ in default access: private for class, public for struct. Their underlying mechanisms are the same. Private access restricts ordinary use at compile time; it neither encrypts memory nor creates a security boundary. The laboratory hides the field and exposes operations. This is a code organization rule rather than secret protection.
An interface declaration should provide the types, parameters and results a client needs. Do not return a mutable reference to the internal quantity: a caller could assign minus one and bypass validation. In larger types a pointer or view also needs a lifetime contract. For now the observer returns a small int by value.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Const and observation
A quantity() const method can be called through const Stock&. Inside it, this points to a const object, so ordinary field assignment is forbidden. The method marks an observation and helps the compiler catch accidental changes. receive and ship are not const because a successful call changes domain state.
Const does not automatically imply thread safety or the absence of external effects. A method could write to cout, and mutable fields follow special rules. Our observer deliberately performs no input or output. That is a stronger design agreement than the keyword alone. A free printing function can use a const reference without owning the object.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Related fields and domain atomicity
Window has two fields with the invariant low_≤high_. Two independent setters could create an invalid intermediate state when changing [0,0] to [2,7]. reset(a,b) accepts both values, checks their relationship and only then assigns them. This atomicity concerns domain meaning; it does not describe synchronization between threads.
After reset(2,7), the worked example calls reset(9,1) and receives false. contains(4) remains true, while contains(8) is false. This checks preservation as well as rejection. Validation before small nonthrowing assignments suffices here. Operations that allocate memory need a separate exception guarantee analysis later in the module.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Choosing an error result
A bool works when a caller only needs to know whether an operation succeeded. If callers must distinguish insufficient stock from a negative argument, introduce a result enum or a structure with an error code. Do not encode failure as a valid quantity: zero can be a normal stock level. Exceptions follow resource management later in this module.
An operation rejection and an input syntax error belong to different layers. A negative amount is a correctly parsed int but is rejected by Stock. A letter in place of an amount fails parsing and produces invalid. Classify the error before deciding which layer has enough information to handle it. This improves messages and test stability.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Executing commands step by step
Input contains n pairs: a plus or minus sign and an integer amount. After validating all pairs, the application creates Stock and executes commands in order. Receiving eight, shipping nine and shipping three produces states zero, eight, eight, five, with one rejection. Reordering commands can change the result; these are events, not an unordered collection of numbers.
receive checks n<0 before comparing n to the remaining capacity. ship checks n<0 and n>quantity_. No rejected path writes the field. Locate that property in the program and create a separate test for each condition. A maximum-int case demonstrates one safe rejection rather than promising arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
A negative compilation check
A small diagnostic example tries to read s.quantity_ from main. Compilation must fail because that member is private. This is an expected compile error, not an executable demonstration or a runtime failure. Compare it with s.quantity(), which uses the public contract and leaves state unchanged.
Keep these checks separate from the working application. Do not add a second main to the same executable or leave the intentional error in its primary file. Diagnostic wording varies between compilers; the access restriction is what matters. Memory inspection or reinterpret_cast would not test the interface and is not an appropriate workaround.

records.title: Classes, interfaces and state
records.text:
Reviewing an interface
Present a transition table and explain why every public method preserves the invariant. Add a requirement that partial shipping is either forbidden or explicitly supported. Show the changed contract and tests before editing implementation. Preserving an interface does not mean preserving every accidental behaviour that an earlier implementation happened to expose.
Also check const usage and the absence of a mutable alias to the field. A good interface makes invalid actions difficult and valid actions understandable. The next lesson answers the remaining lifecycle questions: how an object obtains its initial state, which parts are created first and when automatic cleanup occurs.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
Literal: A value written directly in source: 60, 0b1010, 'A', or "done".
const: For the simple objects in this lesson, prevents changing the value after initialization by ordinary assignment.
constexpr: In our integer constant declaration, requires a valid constant-expression initializer and makes the object const.
Comment: A source explanation rather than an executable statement; it must stay accurate when code changes.
Magic number: A literal whose purpose or unit is unclear where it is used. Not every literal is automatically bad.
Escape sequence: A notation for a special character within a literal, such as \n for newline or \\ for a backslash.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
Write values precisely, name immutable quantities, and use comments to explain decisions.
Distinguish a literal, a named object, and an explanatory comment.
Use const and simple constexpr without confusing immutability with evaluation time.
Read digit separators, binary notation, char, strings, and basic escape sequences.
Replace unexplained conversion factors and check the unit contract with several values.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
A literal, an object, and a name are different
In const int lessonMinutes = 25;, 25 is a literal and lessonMinutes is a name; the declaration creates an int object with that initial value. A type determines values and operations. int suffices for the small whole numbers here; a fuller type treatment follows next.
Two occurrences of 60 may mean seconds per minute and an age limit. Combining them under one name merely because the numbers match is wrong. Choose a name for the domain meaning. secondsPerMinute expresses a minutes-to-seconds factor; generalValue does not.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
const prevents object mutation, not a timing promise
const int lessonMinutes = 25; initializes a simple integer object whose value cannot later be replaced by ordinary assignment such as lessonMinutes = 30;. Initialization supplies the first value; assignment tries to replace an existing one. The negative example below deliberately tests a build error.
const alone does not require the initial value to be known at compile time: it may be obtained during execution. A fixed number in our example does not turn const into a universal instruction to precompute. We do not introduce runtime input merely to demonstrate this; its rules belong in the standard-I/O lesson.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
constexpr in a small, explicit example
constexpr int secondsPerHour = 60 * 60; requires a valid constant expression as its initializer. The operands are known, the multiplication is permitted, and 3600 fits in int. The object is also const, so later assignment is prohibited. This makes the intention explicit for fixed conversion factors.
This is a rule about allowed expressions, not an optimizer stopwatch. Do not claim that const is always slower than constexpr or that every occurrence forces a separate build-time operation. We are not writing constexpr functions, #define macros, or metaprograms here.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
Numeric notation: value and readability
1024 and 1'024 denote the same value: an apostrophe within the number separates digits and is not printed. A separator cannot be placed arbitrarily before the first or after the last digit. 1,024 is not the same literal; a comma has other C++ roles. Decimal fractions in source use a dot, as in 2.5.
The 0b prefix introduces binary notation: 0b1010 = 8 + 2 = 10. Ordinary std::cout output of int remains decimal and prints 10. Hexadecimal uses 0x, but this lesson is not a full number-base course. Avoid 010 when you mean ten: a leading zero introduces octal notation. Prefer decimal notation for ordinary quantities.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
One character, a string, and a backslash
In const char grade = 'A';, char is a character type for one code unit, and single quotes introduce an ordinary character literal. "A" in double quotes is a string literal, with a different type and representation. A word does not fit in one char. Ordinary char is not a container for every Unicode character: a Russian letter encoded in UTF-8 can occupy multiple bytes.
\n denotes newline, \t a tab, \\ one backslash, and \" a quote within a string. The path example escapes the backslash in C:\temp; otherwise \t would become a tab. Quotes and backslashes in source are notation rather than an instruction to print every source character. Predict actual stdout instead of copying the source literal.

records.title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
records.text:
Replacing a magic number without unnecessary abstraction
Record the original result. Determine the factor’s meaning, declare a name, replace corresponding uses, and compare output. Not every zero or newline needs a separate name. Naming helps when it explains a domain rule or prevents inconsistent changes.
Names do not validate units automatically. After the minutes-to-seconds review, test 0, 15, and 40 minutes again. The diagram connects the domain concept, value notation, and use. It does not prove when a compiler evaluated an expression.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Composition: Containing collaborating objects and delegating work to them.
Inheritance: A language-defined relationship between a derived and a base type.
Substitutability: A derived type satisfying the complete base contract.
Virtual operation: Enabling dynamic dispatch through a base interface.
Abstract class: A type with a pure virtual operation that cannot be instantiated directly.
Override: A request for compile-time verification of overriding.
Slicing: Copying only the base portion of a derived object into a base value.
Dynamic cast: A checked polymorphic cast with a defined failure outcome.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Choose a suitable dependency and implement substitutable strategies with correct ownership.
Draw Report and Rate using composition.
Predict a call through Rule&.
Change const in override and inspect compilation failure.
Check both pointer dynamic_cast outcomes.
Add a third strategy.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Start with composition
Composition means containing other objects and delegating part of the work to them. Report stores Rate and calls rate_.apply from total. This is a has-a relationship rather than an is-a relationship. For a fixed set of dependencies it is simpler and needs no virtual functions, dynamic allocation or common base class.
Begin with a concrete requirement: changing a scoring strategy while retaining the caller. If variants are few and known at build time, a field, function parameter or template may suffice. Dynamic polymorphism is useful when implementation is selected at runtime and a client uses a shared contract. Choose it from requirements rather than treating it as an obligatory endpoint of object orientation.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
The base interface contract
Rule declares virtual int apply(int) const=0. Virtual dispatch selects an implementation through a base reference or pointer. The =0 makes the operation pure virtual and the class abstract: Rule cannot be instantiated directly. A derived Regular or Urgent supplies a matching implementation to become concrete.
A contract includes more than a signature: valid arguments, result meaning and effect restrictions should be common to the implementations. If a client supplies any n between zero and one hundred, both strategies must handle the entire range. A derived type accepting only values below ten violates substitutability even if its code compiles.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Override and final
override asks the compiler to verify that a method actually overrides a virtual base operation. Omitting const or changing a parameter type can instead declare a different member that hides the base name rather than overriding it. The example repeats int apply(int) const override explicitly. final prevents further derivation from a class or further overriding of a marked virtual method.
Do not add final without a reason if extensions are expected. A closed concrete strategy usefully demonstrates the interface boundary here. Nonvirtual operations are selected from the expression's static type; inheritance alone does not make them dynamically dispatched. Distinguish overloading, name hiding and overriding by their actual conditions.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Ownership through a base type
std::unique_ptr<Rule> can own an Urgent, while r->apply(n) selects Urgent's implementation. Deleting through that owning base pointer requires a suitable virtual base destructor. The interface therefore contains virtual ~Rule()=default. This connects exclusive ownership with destruction of the complete derived object.
The course does not execute deletion through an unsuitable nonvirtual base. Such a violation may cause undefined behaviour and is not an acceptable experiment. An observing Rule* need not own the object at all. Label the owner separately from an interface reference so dynamic method selection does not hide cleanup responsibility.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Slicing and value semantics
Passing a derived object as a base value copies only its base portion: slicing. An abstract Rule prevents such construction entirely, which is useful. A concrete base might allow compilation while losing derived behaviour. Polymorphic parameters therefore commonly use const Rule& or Rule* rather than values.
Do not use vector<Base> to hold heterogeneous derived objects. A vector<unique_ptr<Base>> can hold different owners when runtime dispatch is justified. For a small closed set of alternatives, the variant introduced in Module 3 may be appropriate. Compare costs, ownership needs and client complexity before choosing a representation.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
RTTI checks an assumption
dynamic_cast<Derived*>(basePointer) checks a polymorphic object's dynamic type and returns nullptr on mismatch. The laboratory intentionally checks both outcomes for Urgent. Never dereference the cast result before checking it. This demonstrates the mechanism, while the actual score still uses the common apply operation.
A long chain of dynamic_cast checks often means the client knows too much about implementations. First consider adding an appropriate interface operation or using a closed set of alternatives. Do not use typeid(...).name() as portable output because the spelling is implementation dependent. A failing reference cast throws and is not needed here.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
Laboratory: strategies
Input mode n selects Regular for mode zero and Urgent for mode one. Regular returns n and Urgent returns twice n. The range zero to one hundred keeps multiplication safe. The shared call contains no strategy condition after selection. A second output column records the safe dynamic_cast result for Urgent.
Run both strategies on zero, seven and one hundred, then test invalid input separately. Propose a third strategy without changing the shared invocation. If only selection and the new implementation change, the boundary is useful. Do not claim virtual calls are faster than ordinary calls: the task concerns dependencies, while cost requires measurement.

records.title: Composition, inheritance and polymorphism
records.text:
A design decision rather than dogma
Compare Report with a concrete Rate, a function accepting a callable and a Rule hierarchy. State when implementation is selected, who owns it and which requirements make the choice simpler or harder. Inheritance needs substitutability by contract; reusing two lines of code does not by itself create a subtype relationship.
In the final project Policy separates scoring from Board. Board stores task values and does not inherit from a container. This combines composition with a narrow interface. The next lesson allows operations to fail by exception and requires showing that owners clean up and the application's promised state remains available.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Constructor: A special function that establishes an object's initial state.
Member initializer list: Constructor syntax specifying direct initialization of bases and members.
Explicit constructor: A constructor declaration restricting implicit conversions.
Destructor: A special function for completing object lifetime and owned cleanup.
Declaration order: The order controlling initialization of nonstatic members.
Scope: A program region in which a name is available under lookup rules.
Deleted operation: An operation marked =delete whose use is rejected at compile time.
Subobject: A base or member whose lifetime participates in the complete object's lifetime.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Trace construction of object parts and automatic cleanup in reverse order.
List the Machine event order.
Compare initialization and body assignment.
Justify the Lease counter lifetime.
Add a third nested scope.
Explain why Lease copying is forbidden.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Initialization precedes the body
A constructor establishes an object's initial state. Its name matches the class and it has no return type. In Level(int n):value_(n), the part after the colon is a member initializer list. The field is created with n directly. Assignment inside the body happens later, after the member has already had to be created.
Prefer direct initialization, especially for const members, references and types without a default constructor. An uninitialized built-in int can hold an indeterminate value that must not be read. A =0 field initializer supplies a useful default, but does not replace validation of domain requirements on constructor arguments.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Declaration order controls initialization
Members are initialized in their declaration order inside the class, regardless of their order in the initializer list. The constructor body executes afterwards. Machine therefore creates a, then b, then prints ready. Rearranging a and b in the initializer list is not a way to change their lifetimes.
If the second member needs the first during construction, declare the dependency earlier. Fix a compiler warning about reordered initialization instead of ignoring it. Do not demonstrate the rule by reading a member whose lifetime has not begun. A safe trace prints identifiers of initialized parts and reveals order without undefined behaviour.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Explicit construction and caller intent
A one-argument constructor can participate in an implicit conversion when its declaration permits it. explicit prevents that copy-initialization conversion while allowing an explicit Level{7}. Calling show(l) with an existing Level is clear; show(7) in the negative example must fail to compile.
This matters for units, identifiers and resources: the integer seven should not accidentally become seven metres or an opened handle. explicit neither checks a range nor automatically makes a type safe. Separate the decisions about permitted conversions from the decisions about which values satisfy the construction contract.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Destruction reverses construction
A destructor is spelled ~Type() and has no parameters. Automatic objects are destroyed in reverse order of successful construction when their scope ends. The complete object's destructor body runs first, followed by its members in reverse declaration order. The Machine trace therefore ends with stop, minus B, minus A.
Reverse order follows dependencies: a later part may rely on an earlier part and should finish first. Do not manually call the destructor of an ordinary local object; later automatic destruction would make the program incorrect. Scopes, containers and standard-library owners suffice for ordinary course work. Placement new is outside this lesson's requirements.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Owning a resource counter
Lease stores an int& referring to an external active counter. Its constructor increments it and its destructor decrements it. The counter outlives every Lease because it is declared earlier in an outer scope. A reference does not own the integer or extend its lifetime. That is an important precondition of this teaching model.
Copying Lease is deleted with =delete. Otherwise two copies could decrement a counter after just one original increment, violating ownership accounting. We do not implement a custom move yet; that has a separate lesson. A deleted operation is a compile-time prohibition rather than a special result produced while the program runs.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Tracing a nested scope
With mode zero, only a exists: the output contains one inside the scope, one before its end and zero afterwards. With mode one, b is created too; one, two, one, zero shows that b is destroyed after the inner if and a later. Mode two intentionally follows the same path and checks the stated input contract.
Write an event, live-object and active-count table before running. The counter is not a universal memory leak detector, but checks acquire/release pairing in this model. Do not inspect a destroyed b to discover what happened; observe the counter whose lifetime continues. No Lease owners remain after the outer scope ends.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Construction failure and cleanup
If construction of a complete object fails with an exception, that complete object's destructor is not called. Members that were successfully constructed are cleaned up. Throwing is studied later; the design implication already matters: do not leave ownership in an unprotected raw pointer between constructor steps.
Destructors should finish without throwing exceptions. Output in tracing examples makes order visible; it is not a model for complicated cleanup with recoverable failures. Handle a file-saving error in an explicit operation before destruction. Prefer established RAII owners for real resources because they reduce the number of manual release paths.

records.title: Construction and lifetime completion
records.text:
Laboratory and transfer
Save the Lease source and traces for all three permitted modes. Explain declaration order, the beginning of lifetime, scope exit and destruction order as separate events. Change nesting safely and predict the new sequence first. Invalid input must be rejected before any Lease objects are created.
The cumulative Window practicum combines the invariant with initialization of the closed, degenerate interval [0,0], which contains the point zero. Resource discipline next transfers to unique_ptr and standard containers. The goal is not to write a destructor for every class. When members already manage their resources, a user-written destructor is often unnecessary.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Type: Rules for an object’s values and operations; a type does not necessarily encode domain units.
Initialization: Providing an initial value when an object is created. Here every object is explicitly initialized.
Range: The set of representable values: a finite numeric type cannot hold every mathematical number.
Target environment: The environment for which a program is built, including type representation and library; browser Clang/WASM is one particular target.
sizeof: An operator reporting size in C++ bytes. sizeof(char) is 1; CHAR_BIT gives the number of bits in such a byte.
numeric_limits: A standard-library facility exposing arithmetic-type properties of the selected implementation.
Tolerance: An acceptable error chosen for a task, not a universal guarantee of double accuracy.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Choose types by domain and range, initialize them, and record target properties without assuming that int always occupies four bytes.
Choose bool, char, integer, or floating-point types by domain meaning.
Explain initial values, simple brace initialization, and type deduction with auto.
Read sizeof(type), CHAR_BIT, and basic numeric_limits properties without writing templates.
Separate language guarantees, target observations, and example restrictions.
Check an approximate number with an explained tolerance and produce a type report.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Session 1. Start with meaning and range
A registration-open flag fits bool with true/false values. A small attendee count fits int when its range is bounded. char stores one code unit such as the label 'B', not an arbitrary string. double can represent an approximate length such as 2.5 meters. Begin with the possible values and intended operations.
A nonnegative count does not automatically require unsigned: subtraction and mixed-sign arithmetic have rules studied later. unsigned int demonstrates a nonnegative-valued type here rather than protection against all mistakes. signed int permits negatives and is the same type as int. Do not test boundaries by executing signed overflow; that operation is not valid.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Initialize before reading
int itemCount{12}; creates an object with value 12. These braces initialize one quantity rather than define the main body. int itemCount = 12; also supplies an initial value, while list initialization with { } rejects certain narrowing conversions. int count{2.5}; deliberately fails to build instead of silently discarding the fraction this way.
int itemCount; for an ordinary local object does not justify reading it as zero. Our normal examples never read such an object: initialize explicitly. int itemCount{}; gives zero for this scalar type and bool ready{}; gives false. Looking at an uninitialized value is not a safe way to discover a language rule.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
auto deduces a type from the initializer
In auto itemCount = 12;, the compiler deduces int from the integer literal. auto length = 2.5; deduces double. This does not create a quantity that changes type on every assignment: the declared type is fixed. Our simple auto declarations require an initializer. We use the = form here and do not generalize deduction to every braced form.
auto reduces repetition but does not express units or domain limits by itself. lengthMeters communicates more than value. At first, record the type you expect from each literal and verify it by reasoning and diagnostics rather than guessing from the printed number.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Floating-point values are an approximate model
float, double, and long double have finite precision and range. Values such as 0.1 need not be represented exactly in the selected format. Thus 0.1 + 0.2 can differ from the stored value of 0.3 even when short printed output looks identical. One successful equality comparison cannot establish a general rule.
Our experiment compares absolute error with 0.000001. <cmath> supplies std::abs(...), returning the absolute difference for double; parentheses pass the value. <= means no greater than, producing bool, which std::cout prints here as 1 or 0. This is an explained library-call recipe, not a requirement to author functions. The tolerance fits these small values; financial amounts are better designed in integer minor units with a proven range.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Session 2. Size is measured in implementation bytes
sizeof(int) reports a type size in C++ bytes. Its parentheses contain a type name; no int object needs to be created. sizeof(char) is guaranteed to be 1, but CHAR_BIT from <climits> specifies bits per byte and is not universally required to be 8. Minimum-range guarantees do not imply identical byte counts everywhere.
The integer types include short, int, long, and long long. Their sizes are nondecreasing, but neighboring types can occupy equal space. long can occupy 4 bytes on one target and 8 on another without either being wrong. sizeof(void*) measures the size of a pointer type used for addresses; pointer operations come later and are not needed here. This size is not universal either.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Reading numeric_limits as a library recipe
Include <limits>. In std::numeric_limits<int>::max(), <int> selects properties for int, :: selects a member, and max() calls the ready-made library operation returning the maximum. lowest() returns the lowest finite value. For floating-point types, min() instead gives the smallest positive normalized value, so do not substitute it for lowest(). We use a library template without writing one.
is_signed reports whether an arithmetic type permits negative values; the answer for char depends on the implementation. digits counts significant radix digits excluding a sign digit; numeric_limits<T>::radix is the base, which is 2 for integers. Thus digits is not a count of decimal digits. int guarantees at least −32767…32767. Read actual limits rather than overflowing an object to find them.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Portable checks and observations are different results
The limits example prints four ones by checking type properties rather than demanding one exact size. >= means no less than, while == compares equality instead of assigning an initial value. These are explained property checks; a full treatment of logic comes later.
The type report prints actual sizes and limits. Its stdout is labeled as a pinned Clang/WASM sample, not an answer for every computer. Record the target and compiler version with the observation. A phone and PC can run the same WASM target; matching sizes therefore do not establish identical native device models or universal IEEE 754 support in C++.

records.title: Data types: choosing values, initialization, and measuring a target
records.text:
Independent type selection and practicum A
The laboratory uses an attendee count, room code, registration flag, and table length. Explain meaning, unit, domain range, and type choice separately. The room label is one ASCII character; a full room name needs another representation. We bound small counts to 0…1000 and lengths to 0…100 meters as task constraints rather than int or double limits.
Practicum A combines the four lessons in a panel report. The supplied totalLengthCm / centimetersPerMeter line is an explained scaffold: centimetersPerMeter is double and makes the division floating-point. Conversion rules are studied later and need not be derived independently now. Preserve the project and a report of names, units, checks, and target properties. This candidate adds no automatic grading or prerequisite gating.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Cohesion: How closely a module's parts serve one coherent responsibility.
Coupling: The degree to which clients depend on another component's decisions.
Refactoring: Changing structure while preserving agreed observable behaviour.
Dependency injection: Supplying a collaborator explicitly rather than through hidden global access.
Test driver: A separate program that invokes domain code and checks conditions.
ADR: A record of context, alternatives, a design decision and its consequences.
Regression check: Checking that previously agreed results survive a change.
Artifact: A saved work result with explicit provenance and verification.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Build a maintainable application, preserve behaviour through refactoring and defend design choices with tests.
Name main, Board and Policy responsibilities.
Test total on empty and ordinary input.
Extract laboratory domain into cpp/header.
Add a Board copy-independence test.
Write an ADR for virtual Policy.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Maintainability as a checkable property
Maintainability becomes visible when a requirement changes: can a rule be changed locally while the rest remains understandable? Do not judge it solely by class count. The project has Task values, a Board owner, Policy strategies, input parsing and report output. Each represents a decision that may change independently.
Begin with concrete scenarios: a normal score equals minutes and an urgent score doubles them. Add import rejection, unique IDs and export. These requirements define test boundaries. An abstraction without a change example remains a hypothesis, so review includes a small new requirement and an assessment of the affected files.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Cohesion and dependencies
High cohesion means a module's parts serve one understandable responsibility. Low coupling means changing an internal decision does not force changes across many clients. Board validates task invariants without opening files or reading cin. A test can therefore construct a candidate in memory without preparing a browser interface.
Policy reaches total as a const reference. Board neither owns it nor selects the mode; it uses its contract. main owns the concrete strategy through unique_ptr. The signature exposes dependency direction. A global singleton added for convenience would hide test inputs and couple otherwise independent runs.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Refactoring preserves behaviour
Refactoring changes code structure while preserving agreed observable behaviour. First capture the current contract in tests, then move total computation out of main into a domain function and rerun them. Changing output format and internal architecture simultaneously makes a mismatch harder to diagnose.
Do not enshrine every accidental detail of an old implementation. A contract may intentionally change, but document that separately from refactoring. The laboratory fixes line order and messages while leaving function placement flexible. This allows extracting domain code into a header and cpp file without changing results for the same inputs.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
A test driver without magic
A separate driver constructs Board and both Policy types, checks normal and urgent totals, copy independence and replacement failures. checks increases only for a successful condition. Any failed condition prints FAIL and produces a nonzero final exit code. A printed PASS string alone is therefore not sufficient evidence of correctness.
The driver replaces main.cpp while using the same domain.cpp and report.cpp. Two main functions cannot be linked into one executable. In Nexus use a separate project copy or explicitly replace the main file after saving it. includeRoots and translationUnits state the build inputs; a tests directory is not compiled automatically.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
The strong import guarantee
Board::replace takes a candidate by value, validates size, ranges and unique IDs, then swaps. Controlled failure occurs before swap. On exception the original tasks remain and the candidate cleans itself up. Tests include invalid data and injected failure on valid data, because those are different rejection causes.
The guarantee concerns Board state rather than every action in main. Status output and file creation follow the import attempt. The report describes current state even after candidate rejection. This protocol exposes preservation through public observations without accessing private fields or claiming a filesystem transaction.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Files and explicit artifacts
The project reads data/tasks.txt and creates board-report.txt in the run filesystem. The web runtime does not promise to write generated output back into the personal project automatically. After verification use the normal explicit save action for result files. Existence during one run does not establish persistence after restart or on another device.
Export checking includes opening the stream, writing, closing and checking its state after close. File destruction releases the resource, while reporting success requires an explicit error check. A missing input file, an empty file and a file containing zero tasks are three different cases and should remain distinct.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
An ADR and alternative review
A short ADR records context, alternatives, a decision and consequences. Compare an open vector plus functions with private Board state, a concrete policy with a virtual interface, and immediate mutation with candidate preparation. Explain which requirement justifies the added complexity and what you would choose for a smaller application.
Arguments should refer to requirements and checkable properties. A pattern name or customary practice is insufficient. State limits: up to twenty tasks, integer minutes, no network or GUI, and explicitly saved exports. Neither this architecture nor its tests prove arbitrary production readiness; they provide a reproducible foundation for subsequent work.

records.title: Design, testability and refactoring
records.text:
Defending the cumulative project
Deliver sources, input files, actual stdout, the saved report, results from the separate driver and an ADR. A teacher or partner then chooses an unseen case within the allowed domain and a small requirement change. For example, add a scoring strategy and show which files and tests actually needed changes.
Completion should not depend on matching the reference source text. Explain the invariant, ownership, independent copy, polymorphic call, failure guarantee and template constraint. Module 6 builds on these foundations for application architecture and events. A later course-wide assessment should integrate modules rather than replace their practice with one final quiz.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Exception: Transfer of control with an error object to a matching handler.
Throw: An expression initiating an exceptional path or rethrowing an exception.
Catch handler: An exception handler selected by type-matching rules.
Stack unwinding: Cleanup of constructed automatic objects in exited scopes.
Basic guarantee: Preservation of invariants without resource leaks after failure.
Strong guarantee: No observable change to the specified state after failure.
Commit: The final step publishing prepared replacement state.
Rethrow: A bare throw; propagates the current exception and preserves its type.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Execute real throw/catch and justify cleanup and state preservation on failure.
Trace Guard before entering catch.
Distinguish basic, strong and nonthrowing guarantees.
Check mode zero and one.
Explain moving throw after swap.
Add a full-snapshot preservation test.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Two ways to report an error
A bool or explicit result type works for an expected rejection that a caller should examine immediately. An exception transfers control to a matching handler along the call stack. Choose according to the contract and the layer able to handle the problem. This is not a division into good and bad errors, or a reason to throw at every if statement.
std::runtime_error and std::invalid_argument are standard exception types declared by stdexcept. A throw starts an exceptional path and ordinary execution after that point stops. A try block surrounds the operation and catch receives a matching error object. This lesson injects controlled failures instead of relying on accidental memory exhaustion, making results reproducible.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Matching a handler
catch(const std::exception& e) observes an exception through a const reference, avoiding copying and slicing. Put a specific handler before its general base handler, otherwise the general one accepts the exception first. catch(...) accepts any type without exposing a typed object and therefore needs an explicit handling policy.
Do not catch everything merely to print success: that hides failure from the caller. Decide whether handling retries an operation, reports rejection or propagates the exception. what() is useful diagnostically, but its wording is not always stable for tests. These contracts compare application-defined messages rather than implementation-specific library wording.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Stack unwinding and RAII
As control transfers from throw to a matching handler, fully constructed automatic objects in exited scopes are destroyed. This is stack unwinding. Guard increments active during construction and decrements it in its destructor. After throw the handler sees active zero: cleanup precedes entering catch. This is an actual exception path rather than an early return with similar output.
If construction fails, the complete object's destructor is not invoked, but already constructed members are destroyed. Resources should therefore enter RAII ownership immediately. Throwing from a destructor during unwinding can cause terminate. The teaching owners use nonthrowing cleanup; recoverable export failures belong to an explicit operation before destruction.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Three guarantee levels
The basic guarantee preserves invariants and avoids resource leaks, while allowing state to change after failure. The strong guarantee additionally promises no observable state change on failure. A nonthrowing guarantee promises that no exception escapes the operation. A guarantee is meaningful only when its operation boundary and observable properties are specified.
The strong guarantee does not roll back the outside world. Restoring a vector cannot erase a message already sent or a line already printed. Store's guarantee concerns values_. Its caller prints status after the operation finishes. The project's Board guarantee is distinct from exporting a report to a file.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Prepare and commit
Store::replace first copies the current vector into candidate, then appends nine. All potentially throwing preparation happens without changing values_. The injected throw is also before commit. A final swap of these vector<int> objects with their ordinary allocator does not throw and replaces state. The temporary then cleans up the former contents.
With mode zero the sum becomes twelve. With mode one it remains three and active returns to zero. In a richer model, test the strong guarantee by comparing the entire observable snapshot rather than just a sum: distinct data can have equal sums. The final project also checks task count and the exact report.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Rethrowing and noexcept
A bare throw; inside catch propagates the current exception while preserving its dynamic type. throw e; can create a new base copy and lose derived information. The second example catches out_of_range through a base reference, rethrows and reaches a specific outer handler. The type actually crosses two call levels.
noexcept is an interface promise rather than a recovery mechanism. If an exception escapes such a function, terminate is invoked; an ordinary outer catch cannot rescue the violation. Do not run termination as an ordinary lesson example. Test safe boundaries instead: a domain operation throws before commit and main handles it while exposing preserved state.

records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Runtime and honest results
This lesson needs a runtime with genuine standard exception support. Code Studio uses Clang/WASI with EH; native execution alone does not prove browser execution. Verification compiles and runs the same sources through both paths. Printing caught without executing throw/catch would not demonstrate exception support.
If an older browser reports a provider limitation, that is not a learner error on the throw line. Do not rewrite exceptions as return codes to claim this outcome. A compatible browser update and a separate native run provide different evidence. Offline compilation must first be prepared through the normal flow; an available lesson text alone does not ensure it.
