records.title: Exceptions and error guarantees
records.text:
Laboratory and cumulative practice
Save both laboratory runs: successful replacement and failure before commit. Record state before and after, plus resource counts. Explain why moving throw after swap would destroy the strong guarantee even if no resource leaked. This is a safe reasoning counterexample; the working implementation should retain its original promise.
The cumulative practicum combines a virtual strategy with an exception for an invalid argument. After rejection, saved remains seven. Add your own preservation check and explain the caller's policy. Templates come next. They do not have exceptions as a hard prerequisite, although they follow them in the module's teaching sequence.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Expression: A combination of operands and operations producing a typed value in our calculations.
Operand: A value or nested expression to which an operation applies.
Precedence: A rule for grouping operators when parentheses are absent.
Associativity: Grouping for operators at the same precedence level, not a general evaluation-order promise.
Intermediate quantity: A named calculation result that can be observed and checked separately.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Break a formula into operands, predict the result, and rewrite a dense line as verifiable intermediate calculations.
Identify operands, operator, type, and value in a simple expression.
Use parentheses and basic multiplicative versus additive precedence.
Distinguish grouping from operand evaluation order.
Extract intermediate quantities while preserving result and units.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Start with value and type
In count * unitPriceCents the names are operands and * multiplies them. When both are int and the result is representable, the expression also has type int. An expression need not mutate its operands: reading two values and producing a result differs from assignment.
int total = count * unitPriceCents; initializes total from the expression. std::cout << total; observes the value. This separates domain calculation, storage, and formatting. Annotate units: items × cents per item = cents.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Precedence determines a grouping tree
2 + 3 * 4 groups multiplication inside addition: it corresponds to 2 + (3 * 4), giving 14. (2 + 3) * 4 explicitly selects another calculation and gives 20. Parentheses do not request speed; they specify expression structure.
At this level + and − group left: 20 - 5 - 3 means (20 - 5) - 3, not 20 - (5 - 3). You need not memorize the entire operator table now. Apply the levels in use and add parentheses that clarify intention. Parentheses cannot rescue a domain formula that was chosen incorrectly.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Grouping is not chronological order
The tree 2 + (3 * 4) describes value dependencies. It does not establish that the left operand always executes first in arbitrary C++. Our calculations have no changing operands, so stdout does not expose this distinction yet.
Increment and complex calls come later. Keep one understandable effect in its own statement. We do not run i++ + ++i as a puzzle: this style obscures sequencing rules and can have undefined behavior. Experimenting does not make a dangerous expression valid.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Intermediate names expose the formula
unitPriceCents * count + shippingCents can be split into goodsCents and totalCents. Goods and shipping can then be checked separately. This does not create a dynamically linked formula: each statement computes its value when executed, as in the variables lesson.
Keep types and statement dependencies and do not introduce hidden rounding. The demonstrated split preserves the bounded integer calculation. Arbitrary rearrangements of floating-point operations can change rounding; this is not permission for every algebraic rewrite.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
A block groups a stage, not arithmetic
A nested block can limit temporary names. If a result is needed outside, declare and initialize the outer result first, then assign the calculation to it inside. Declaring another result inside hides the outer object rather than updating it.
Expression parentheses (a + b) and block braces { ... } have different roles. State what is grouped: formula operands or statements and scope. This is more useful than mechanically adding brackets everywhere.

records.title: Expressions and operators: grouping, values, and clear steps
records.text:
Checking readability through behavior preservation
Before editing, record the contract and several data sets. After extracting intermediate quantities compare the whole stdout and explain each stage in domain terms. Agreement only at zero price is a weak test that may fail to distinguish formulas.
The diagram shows one selected grouping. It is not a parser and does not establish arbitrary program evaluation order. The laboratory needs source, checks, and an equivalence explanation rather than merely an attractive tree screenshot.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
Runtime FS: the isolated file set for one program execution.
Artifact: an execution result that can be inspected and explicitly saved.
ifstream: an input file stream.
ofstream: an output file stream.
Truncation: discarding previous contents under the selected open mode.
Roundtrip: export, explicit saving, and a fresh verified import.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
Validate an import, create a report, and separately confirm transfer of runtime output into the project.
Explain: A file as a resource
Trace: The format is an interface
Justify: The Nexus virtual filesystem
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not open the input with ofstream before validation. Do not assume ambient runtime persistence between runs.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
A file as a resource
ifstream from <fstream> reads a file; ofstream writes one. Construction associates the stream with a path, and destruction closes the resource. Check opening through bool(stream). RAII cleanup is useful, but successful opening does not guarantee every later operation succeeds.
A regular ofstream may truncate an existing file. Do not open an input file for writing before validating its data. The lab writes a separate report.txt and preserves records.txt.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
The format is an interface
A text format defines encoding, delimiters, field counts, and bounds. The lab records.txt contains one integer in -1000…1000 per line, at most 100 lines of 200 bytes. An empty file is valid; a blank line is malformed.
Parse each line using a local istringstream and reject trailing data. Do not save a struct by dumping its memory: padding, type sizes, and byte order may differ. A textual contract is easier to verify manually and with two compilers.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
Read and write failures
A missing file produces missing; a malformed record produces invalid. Do not treat every stopped getline as normal completion: check bad and unexpected failure without eof. A partial import must not generate a successful final report.
After writing, call close and check the stream: flushing can fail late. The lab distinguishes write-error from invalid. This does not promise atomic replacement after a crash; that needs a separate storage strategy.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
The Nexus virtual filesystem
A program sees relative files supplied with its request. Absolute paths, .., and system directories are unavailable. Every run receives a fresh runtime filesystem; a previous run’s file does not appear automatically in the next. stdin is not a substitute for testing file input.
Limits are 128 files, 512 KiB per file, 2 MiB for input and runtime files, and 2 MiB of writes per run. Exceeding them is a provider limitation distinct from an algorithm defect. Do not raise quotas to bypass an exercise.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
An artifact and a personal project
The result panel lists new or changed runtime files. Downloading saves a separate copy. Saving text results transfers them into the VFS only through an explicit action and when no conflicting edits exist. A program cannot silently replace source code.
A binary result downloads as bytes rather than becoming an editor text file. A conflict preserves the project source. For another run, explicitly save a permitted text file, then rerun the reader and compare contents.

records.title: Files: formats, failures, and explicit saving
records.text:
Roundtrip evidence
Separately test a missing file, a valid import, malformed data, export, and report.txt contents. Then confirm saving into the project and a fresh run. Reading within the same run does not establish that final step.
Use synthetic data only; do not put keys or personal work into evidence. Next, a linked list demonstrates node-resource management, while the final project combines records, commands, tests, and file formats.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Source code: Program text checked and translated by a compiler before execution.
The main entry point: The special function that begins the user-written part of a normal hosted C++ program after runtime setup.
stdout: The standard output stream; Code Studio displays its content in the result area.
Declaration with initialization: In int boxes = 3;, a named integer object is created with the initial value 3.
Exit code: A status value returned when the program ends; 0 indicates success and is not a printed character.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Build a program, explain every part of its scaffold, and produce a small report with predictable output.
Explain #include, int main(), braces, std::cout, <<, a string, ;, and return 0.
Distinguish source, build diagnostics, stdout, and an exit code.
Build a report from labels and named integer quantities.
Predict output and verify a repair by changing one thing at a time.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Session 1. Define an observable result first
Our first task is to print exactly Hello, C++! followed by a newline. Write that expectation before running. The editor contains source; the result panel shows consequences of execution. Similar text in both places does not make them the same thing.
Open main.cpp in Code Studio, insert the first example, and select Run. Leave stdin, the separate field for standard input, empty: this program reads nothing. The first run may download the pinned Clang/WASM compiler. Wait for the build result, then locate the output line and exit code.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Why begin with #include <iostream>?
The #include preprocessing directive names the standard <iostream> header. It makes declarations for stream input and output available, including std::cout. It is not a print command and does not require an iostream.cpp file beside main.cpp.
The directive line does not end with ;. The environment supplies the corresponding library during the build. Include headers for facilities you actually use. The diagnostic example without <iostream> should fail to build.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
main is an explained scaffold, not a hidden functions prerequisite
In int main(), main names the entry point, int is the return-status type, and empty parentheses specify the no-parameter form. The body between { and } contains statements. In a hosted environment it runs after runtime setup. Functions will receive a full treatment later; for now explain the scaffold rather than inventing additional functions.
return 0; ends main successfully. It does not print 0. A special rule for main gives the same successful status when execution reaches its closing brace without an explicit return. Do not generalize that rule to every function. Most examples keep return explicit to make the status visible.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Reading std::cout << "text"
std is the standard-library namespace; :: selects cout within it. std::cout represents standard output. In this expression, << inserts the following value into the stream. The same symbol can mean a bit shift elsewhere, but the stream on the left determines its use here. You do not need operator-overloading theory yet.
Double quotes delimit a string literal: they appear in source but are not printed. Inside a literal, \n denotes a newline; two source characters describe one control character. A chain of << operations can print a label, a number, and a newline. Spaces are not inserted automatically.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Semicolons and indentation serve different purposes
Output statements and return end with ;. A source newline does not replace it. Braces delimit the body of main; its closing brace needs no semicolon. Indentation helps people see structure but cannot repair a missing delimiter.
Start with the first meaningful build diagnostic and inspect the indicated line and the previous line. A compiler may detect a problem after its cause. Repair one defect, rebuild, and then evaluate the output. Exact diagnostic wording depends on the compiler and is not part of the program output contract.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Session 2. From a fixed line to named quantities
In int boxes = 3;, int supplies an integer type, boxes is the author-chosen name, and = 3 supplies the initial value. The object stores a value and its name lets later statements use it. This is a small scaffold; type ranges and scope are separate lessons. All values here are small enough for int.
int totalItems = boxes * itemsPerBox; evaluates the current values when totalItems is created. It is not a spreadsheet formula that stays linked forever. Editing initial values and rerunning the whole program performs a new calculation. The labels boxes= and items= make the output understandable without memorizing column positions.

records.title: Your first C++ program: from source to a verifiable report
records.text:
Verification record and model limits
For each experiment record source, empty stdin, expected stdout, actual stdout, and exit code. Distinguish a missing final newline from a wrong number. Calculate the product independently; copying the same mistaken formula into a check is not independent verification.
The diagram below explains stages and does not execute a compiler. Next changes the stage explanation; real execution occurs in Code Studio. Saving a file or answering a question does not prove a build or mastery. Keep a copy before replacing work in your own project.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Decision node: A conditional split with explicitly labeled outcomes.
Execution path: The sequence of nodes visited by a particular input.
Branch coverage: Tests that exercise each alternative outcome of a decision.
Diagram invariant: A property assumed to be true when control reaches a particular node.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
A flowchart is not decorative artwork. It shows how an algorithm chooses actions and which path a particular input follows.
Follow directed control-flow edges.
Distinguish actions, decisions, input/output and start/end.
Trace all branches, including boundaries.
Translate diagrams into C++ and concrete tests.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
The transition matters more than the shape
Start and end define procedure boundaries. An action modifies state; input/output interacts with the outside world; a decision chooses a path. Connections need clear direction.
Without labeled true/false branches, a reader must guess which path to follow. A sound flowchart allows manual execution without consulting its author.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Order validation before shipping price
Consider a delivery policy: negative order totals are invalid, orders totaling at least 1000 get free delivery, and smaller valid orders pay 150. Validation therefore precedes the threshold check.
Moving checks into the wrong order can apply a fee to invalid orders. The diagram makes the policy explicit before C++ code is written.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Tracing inputs and covering branches
For -1 the result is invalid; for 999 the delivery fee is 150; for 1000 it is free. These exercise distinct execution paths.
Testing only one friendly input does not establish branch behavior. Boundary cases distinguish > from >= and catch off-by-one defects.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Decompose complex charts
A high-level diagram reading 'validate order → calculate total → produce receipt' is usually clearer than a hundred small rectangles. Move inner details into subprocedures.
Specify the inputs and outputs of each component. A diagram neither replaces an interface contract nor removes the need for tests.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Make visual models accessible and truthful
A diagram's labels must match the conditions in the executable code. On small screens, the same transitions need an accessible textual explanation.
An interactive diagram is still a model rather than a compiler result. Compare it against actual outputs in Code Studio.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Two tariffs, two distinct contracts
The interactive model uses an order-amount threshold; the laboratory uses distance. Do not carry x≥1000 into the kilometre program. Distances 1..5 cost 100, 6 costs 120, and 8 costs 160. The laboratory flow is input → valid distance? → distance>5? → extra charge → output. Label both yes and no exits at each decision.

records.title: Flowcharts as testable execution models
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
The laboratory accepts distance from 1 to 1000000; other values produce invalid.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
Invariant: a statement preserved by each loop iteration.
Termination variant: a bounded quantity that decreases on every iteration.
Iteration: one execution of a loop body.
Accumulator: state collecting the result of multiple steps.
Half-open range: a range including its left bound and excluding its right bound.
Off-by-one: a one-step error caused by an incorrect boundary.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
Repeat a known number of steps and explain the state before and after every iteration.
Explain: The three header parts
Trace: A half-open interval rather than a guess
Justify: Accumulators and ranges
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not reset the sum in the body. Test < versus <= only with a safe scalar counter.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
The three header parts
for(init; condition; update) runs init once and tests condition before every iteration. update follows the body. If the first condition is false, the body never runs, making n=0 a natural case.
In for(int i=0; i<n; ++i), i exists in the condition, body, and update but not after the loop. It denotes the next index to process. The iteration count is n for a bounded nonnegative n.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
A half-open interval rather than a guess
The index range [0,n) includes 0 and excludes n, giving exactly n positions. Values 1 through n can use i=1; i<=n, but mixing the first version’s start with the second version’s condition changes the count.
For n=3, the body sees i=0,1,2; the i=3 check terminates the loop. That final value is tested but not processed. Confusing a check with an execution often causes an off-by-one error.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
An invariant as a short proof
For the sum of n integers starting at zero, the invariant is: before each iteration, sum contains the sum of [0,i). At i=0 the range is empty, so sum=0. After sum+=i and ++i, the claim holds for the larger boundary.
When i==n, the invariant yields the required result. Prove termination separately: n-i is nonnegative before the body and decreases by one. A correct invariant cannot guarantee termination if the counter never advances.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
Accumulators and ranges
Initialize an accumulator before the loop and update it inside. Resetting it on every iteration retains only the final contribution. With n<=1000 and values between -1000 and 1000, the absolute sum is at most 1000000.
Use long long for broader bounds and justify intermediate values before addition. A larger type does not make unbounded input safe. Handle an extraction failure inside the loop instead of repeatedly adding an old value.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
break and continue
break exits the nearest loop. continue skips the rest of the body but still performs a for loop’s update. In filtering it can separate an unsuitable element, but it must not bypass the operation that obtains the next item.
Nested loops have separate counters; break exits only the inner loop. A complete r by c traversal performs r*c iterations. Establish dimension bounds before multiplying and estimating cost.

records.title: The for loop: invariants, boundaries, and cost
records.text:
Measuring work
A linear traversal performs work proportional to n: O(n), with O(1) extra memory for a fixed number of accumulators. This describes growth, not milliseconds or an exact instruction count.
Test n=0, n=1, the maximum n, and a failure midway through input. For a small n, record i, the condition, and sum before and after the body. Next, while will handle a stream whose length is not given in advance.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
Manipulator: an operation changing stream formatting or state.
Minimum width: a field can grow and does not truncate the value.
fixed: floating formatting with a fixed number of fractional digits.
precision: significant or fractional digit count according to formatting mode.
fill: a persistent field-padding character.
Exact monetary unit: an integral minor-unit count instead of an approximate decimal fraction.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
Specify a reproducible textual report and explain which stream settings persist.
Explain: A value is separate from its text
Trace: fixed and setprecision
Justify: State manipulators
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not confuse setprecision with storage precision. Do not expect setw to truncate long values.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
A value is separate from its text
double stores a binary value; fixed and setprecision choose textual representation without increasing calculation precision. Money can use integral minor units and print whole and fractional parts separately.
Specify units, permitted signs, rounding, and separators. The lab price is an integer number of cents in 0…100000, quantity is 0…1000, and total is at most 100000000 cents. Integer arithmetic avoids decimal representation error.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
fixed and setprecision
With fixed, setprecision(2) from <iomanip> requests two digits after the decimal point. Without fixed, precision normally means significant digits. The setting affects subsequent insertions until changed.
std::defaultfloat restores general floating formatting but does not reset every stream flag. An independent report can use its own ostringstream with explicit settings. Here first trace cout’s state.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
Width, fill, and alignment
setw(n) sets the minimum width of the next formatted field; longer values are not truncated. setfill('0') changes the fill character persistently. std::left and std::right also persist.
To print five cents, output 0, a dot, and the remainder with setw(2) and setfill('0'), yielding 0.05. Repeat setw for another field. Field width is a representation rule, not protection against oversized input.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
State manipulators
boolalpha prints true/false rather than 1/0 until noboolalpha. hex selects hexadecimal integer output; dec restores decimal. Avoid leaving an unexpected mode for the next report section.
\n adds a newline; endl additionally flushes the buffer. Repeated flushing is usually unnecessary in a batch sandbox. The environment’s overall output limit applies regardless of formatting.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
Locale and portability
A text protocol should specify the decimal point and absence of grouping separators. Do not rely on incidental user locale. The examples explicitly form integer parts and a dot and use ASCII stdout.
Compare exact bytes separately from numeric closeness. 1.5 versus 1.50 may pass a numeric check while violating the interface. Approximate calculations need an explicit tolerance; setprecision does not repair the mathematics.

records.title: Formatted output: values and representations
records.text:
Report checks
Test zero, one minor unit, a whole amount, and the maximum amount. Preserve expected strings including spaces and newlines. For setw, include a value longer than the field to avoid treating width as a length limit.
Check persistent fill and reset width on the next field. Input states require the same discipline next: flags belong to a stream and affect later operations until explicitly handled.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Contract: caller obligations and operation guarantees.
Side effect: an observable change beyond the return value.
Argument: an expression supplied in a function call.
Parameter: a local input name in a function declaration.
Precondition: an obligation before performing an operation.
Postcondition: a guarantee after an operation whose preconditions hold.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Separate validation, computation, and presentation so a small function can be checked without a console.
Explain: Calls and definitions
Trace: Values, references, and const
Justify: Pure computation and side effects
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not assign result before every check succeeds. Do not return a reference to a local variable.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Calls and definitions
In int twice(int value), twice names the function, the first int is the return type, and value is a local parameter. The body runs when called, not when the compiler encounters its definition. return 2*value finishes this invocation and supplies its result to the caller.
Define a teaching function before main so its declaration is visible at the call site. int result=twice(4) supplies the argument 4 and stores the result 8. Calling it does not print anything by itself; output is a separate operation.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Values, references, and const
An int value parameter receives a separate value: changing it does not change the caller’s int. int& binds to the original object and permits mutation. const int& prevents mutation through that reference but neither copies the object nor makes it permanently const.
Small scalar values are usually passed by value. Larger read-only objects can use const references. In the lab, const std::string& checks a string without copying it. A reference must not outlive its owner; never return a reference to a local variable.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Preconditions and postconditions
The twice contract bounds its input so 2*value fits the type. That is straightforward for -1000 through 1000, but not for arbitrary int. A precondition is the caller’s obligation; a postcondition is the guaranteed result property when that obligation holds.
Do not treat malformed external input as a violation that can be ignored. At the boundary, main checks extraction and ranges before an internal function receives values. For an expected rejection, a bool result with an explicitly documented output parameter is useful.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Pure computation and side effects
A calculation function should not secretly read cin or change a global accumulator. The same arguments yield the same result without changing the environment. A unit test can then pass arguments directly and compare the result without replacing the console.
An output reference makes mutation visible in the signature but needs an exact rule: leave it unchanged on false. Calculate into a temporary and assign only on success. This is a simple form of operation atomicity.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Decomposition without unnecessary coupling
Split the task into validation, calculation, and presentation. Each function should answer one question and have a meaningful name. Avoid ten unrelated parameters when one value suffices; a later struct will group related data.
Local variables in separate calls are independent. Returning a result by value is safe; returning a local object’s address is not. Recursion, authored templates, and overloading are unnecessary here and are not hidden lab requirements.

records.title: Functions: parameters, results, and contracts
records.text:
Testing a function separately from input
Build an argument table: lower boundary, a normal value, upper boundary, and nearby rejections. Check that read-only operations leave the original object unchanged and that a false result preserves the output parameter.
Then add integration cases for cin: empty input, a wrong type, and an extra token. A successful unit test does not establish parser correctness. Next, pass a whole sequence to a function using the standard span view.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
Coverage: every input has defined behaviour.
Disjointness: a valid input belongs to exactly one class.
Guard: an early rejection before an operation with a stricter precondition.
Branch: an execution path selected by a condition.
case: a constant selection label inside switch.
Fallthrough: continuing into the next case body without exiting.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
Build a complete input classification and show that every valid case receives exactly one answer.
Explain: A decision starts with a contract
Trace: if, else, and one selected path
Justify: switch for discrete selection
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: At 85 check >= versus >. In a switch inspect each break.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
A decision starts with a contract
A condition selects a path through one program. First list valid inputs, the result for each class, and the rejection policy. A score from 0 to 100 has an invalid class outside the range and separate intervals inside it.
Check extraction from cin before comparing the value. Successfully reading a number does not make it a valid score. Boundary values 0, 59, 60, 84, 85, 100 and their neighbours turn prose requirements into a verifiable table.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
if, else, and one selected path
if evaluates a condition, contextually converts the result to bool, and executes its body when true. else executes only when false. Braces group statements and expose the scope of local variables; use them even for short branches.
Two independent if statements can both execute. An if/else if chain selects the first true branch. For descending thresholds test >=85 before >=60: the earlier failure already establishes the next interval’s upper bound.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
Coverage and disjointness
Draw a number line and mark whether each boundary is included. x>=60 && x<85 denotes a half-open interval. In C++, 60<=x<85 first produces a bool and then compares 0 or 1 with 85; it does not express a mathematical comparison chain.
Guard checks help prevent invalid operations: reject a zero divisor before dividing. Short-circuit && and || were introduced in Module 2; here they support a safety argument rather than hiding several actions inside a condition.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
switch for discrete selection
switch matches an integer or enumeration against constant case labels. It suits command codes but does not replace arbitrary ranges or string comparisons. default handles the remaining values and is especially useful for untrusted input.
A case label does not stop execution. break exits the switch; return exits the function. Without either, control continues into the next case. Sharing a body between labels is valid; an intentional transition between bodies needs explanation and [[fallthrough]].

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
Nesting and clarity
An else binds to the nearest unmatched if. Braces remove ambiguity for the reader. An early invalid return reduces nesting in the main logic: after that guard, the range is known to be valid.
Do not replace a long classification with nested ?: merely to shorten it. The conditional operator suits two simple values; several rejection reasons are clearer as explicit checks. A comment should explain a domain threshold rather than restating >=.

records.title: Branching: decisions, ranges, and switch
records.text:
Checking a decision and the next step
Choose an input that reaches each branch, then test both sides of every threshold and failed extraction. A middle-of-range example cannot detect > substituted for >=; a boundary table can.
Keep a table of input, expected result, and actual result with a short coverage argument. A loop will later repeat the decision for a sequence, multiplying any classification error. Establish one correct step before arranging repetition.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
Prefix ++: For int, increments the object and refers to the updated object.
Postfix ++: For int, produces the previous value and increments the object.
Unevaluated operand: Checked under language rules without ordinary runtime evaluation; the simple sizeof operand is such a case.
Conditional operator ?:: Chooses the second or third operand for evaluation from a bool condition.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
Separate object mutation, expression value, type measurement, and selecting an evaluated branch.
Distinguish prefix/postfix and object state from expression result.
Explain why sizeof(++n) does not increment an ordinary int n.
Use ?: with simple compatible branches.
Keep one update per full statement.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
State and result need separate columns
With int count{3}; int oldValue = count++; count becomes 4 while oldValue receives 3. Next, int newValue = ++count; makes count 5 and gives newValue 5. Keep separate columns for count afterward and expression result so the distinction remains visible.
-- subtracts 1 with the same prefix/postfix distinction. As standalone statements count++; and ++count; leave the same final count because the result is discarded. Choose clarity rather than claiming one form is faster for every type.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
One statement, one clear update
Do not combine multiple updates of one object into a puzzle. Forms such as i++ + ++i can have undefined behavior and are unsuitable prediction experiments. Our updates occupy separate full statements, with output afterward.
Range restrictions remain: ++ on the maximum signed int is not permitted merely because the notation is short. Check preconditions first. We use 3…5 safely inside range and explain dangerous boundaries without execution.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
sizeof obtains information without evaluating its operand
In sizeof(++count) for an ordinary int, the operand is unevaluated and count stays 5. ++count has type int, so its size equals sizeof(int). Compare with == rather than demanding one byte count on every target. This extends the types lesson with an expression rule.
Unevaluated does not mean arbitrary text is valid: sizeof(stillUnknown) fails without a declaration. The compiler needs a valid operand and type. sizeof yields unsigned std::size_t; auto bytes = ... obtains it without an unnecessary cast.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
?: evaluates only the selected branch
condition ? first : second checks the condition and evaluates first if true or second otherwise. With divisor=0 it selects 0 without evaluating 12/divisor. Zero is only a demonstration default, not a complete input-error report.
Both branches must be valid expressions even though only one is selected. Language rules determine the result type; we use two int branches. We avoid mixed signs and advanced value categories. Multi-statement branches are clearer as a separate if, treated fully next module.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
Allocation policy without hidden mutation
requested <= available ? requested : available selects the smaller valid count. A separate assignment reduces available. Two steps expose the rule against issuing more than stock instead of mixing ++ and ?:.
First exclude negatives and values over 100. issued then lies from 0 to available and the remainder is nonnegative. Test requested=0, requested=available, and requested>available. These are distinct contract cases even if two produce the same stdout for a particular stock.

records.title: ++ and --, sizeof and ?: — concise syntax with precise meaning
records.text:
Checking three different mechanisms
For ++ record prior state, result, and final state. For sizeof record count before and after plus size equality. For ?: identify the chosen and skipped branches. A final number alone often hides a wrong explanation.
The diagram is a fixed journal over 3…5. Next does not mutate a live C++ object; execution is checked in Code Studio. Retain predictions made before running so the report identifies the hypothesis actually tested.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Half-open range: Includes first and excludes last; empty when first==last.
Iterator: A navigation object with specified valid operations.
Random access: A category supporting constant-time offsets and distances.
Predicate: A callable whose result acts as a Boolean condition.
Comparator: A strict weak ordering defining which element precedes another.
Capture: Including external values or references in a lambda closure.
Invalidation: An iterator or view becoming invalid after an owner mutation.
Initial accumulator: The value and type from which accumulate begins a fold.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Compose small algorithms while specifying their ranges, destinations and callback behavior.
Justify half-open range boundaries.
Choose an iterator category for an algorithm.
Write a strict comparator and a predicate.
Predict invalidation after vector growth.
Build a copy_if, sort, transform, accumulate pipeline without losing data.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
A container and a traversal position
A container owns and organizes elements; an iterator identifies a position in a sequence. A vector iterator resembles a pointer, but reason through its permitted operations: dereference, advance and comparison. *it is the element, while it is the access mechanism. Copying an iterator does not copy the container.
begin() identifies the first element when one exists; end() is the past-the-end position. An empty container has begin()==end(), a valid empty range. end is not the last element and must not be dereferenced. An algorithm stops before reading it, and a search result must be checked before accessing its element.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Why ranges are half-open
[first,last) includes first and excludes last. Adjacent ranges [a,b) and [b,c) join without duplicating b, and equal boundaries naturally express emptiness. last must be reachable from first through valid advances. Iterators from different vectors do not form a range even if their addresses happen to look nearby.
For a vector, last−first counts elements in a valid range. That does not mean every iterator pair supports subtraction. Name the category and establish that both positions belong to one range first. Diagnose boundary errors on paper and with safe checks rather than deliberately reading beyond end.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Categories constrain algorithms and cost
Input iterators support reading while advancing; forward iterators add multipass traversal, bidirectional iterators add backward steps, and random-access iterators add constant-time movement by an arbitrary distance. Contiguous iterators additionally describe contiguous storage. These are semantic and operational contracts, not identical container implementations.
Ordinary std::sort requires random-access iterators, so a vector fits while an arbitrary linked list does not. find scans forward and needs weaker capabilities. Later, binary search will show how few comparisons can coexist with many forward advances. Algorithm cost must include the cost of its iterator operations.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Search and a predicate
std::find(first,last,value) returns the first equal element or last. std::find_if uses a predicate, a callable bool rule for an element. The example finds the first even number. “First” follows the current range order, so sorting beforehand can change the selected record without changing whether a match exists.
Check it!=end before *it. A vector position can be obtained by subtracting begin only for compatible iterators. A position is not automatically a domain ID: rearrangement and erasure change it. A project’s stable ID belongs in the record; an iterator serves only the current access.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Destination size is not capacity
std::transform reads input and writes transformed elements to a destination. An empty vector has no writable elements at begin, even after reserve: capacity is allocated but size stays zero. Resize the destination or use back_inserter, which appends with push_back. The example chooses a separate output vector that grows through appending.
Do not append to the same vector whose range is being traversed: reallocation can invalidate input iterators. In-place algorithms have specific conditions too; the shown doubling transform writes each item to its existing position. If an operation changes length, define input/output ownership and overlap rules beforehand.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Lambda syntax and capture lifetime
[capture](parameters){body} creates a callable object. In [threshold](int x){return x>=threshold;}, threshold is copied at creation, x arrives at each invocation, and return gives the decision. Value capture keeps the original threshold even if the outer variable later changes. Empty brackets capture no local variables.
[&sum] accesses the original variable, which must remain alive during invocation. This can suit an immediate sequential algorithm, but returning such a lambda requires lifetime reasoning. A sorting predicate must not mutate keys or contradict itself. a>b gives a strict descending order; a>=b does not.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
Accumulation and result types
std::accumulate from <numeric> updates an accumulator sequentially starting at init. init determines the accumulator type: 0 and 0LL are different contracts. The lab uses 0LL for up to 64 doubled values with magnitude at most 10000. Casting an already overflowed sum to long long afterward does not repair it.
An empty range returns init. Explain the arguments and side effects of any custom accumulation operation. Do not silently replace accumulate with a parallel reduction and assume identical ordering, especially for floating point. Here the contract uses sequential integer computation and exact stdout.

records.title: Iterators, STL algorithms and lambdas
records.text:
A pipeline and its engineering checks
The lab validates all input, filters x>=threshold, sorts descending, doubles and sums. State a contract after each stage: selected count is at most n, order follows a>b, and doubling preserves length. Empty output must yield a zero sum and an empty line, not an attempt to read a first item.
Compare the library pipeline with a simple manual implementation on small data. Explain reserve invalidation, index meaning after insertion and the use of separate buffers. Next, search a prepared range: its ordering becomes the following algorithm’s precondition rather than an accidental property of one test input.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
Compilation: Checking and translating C++ source into object representation.
Linking: Resolving cross-module symbols and dependencies into an executable.
Runtime: The environment where a built program reads inputs and produces results.
Debugging: Reproducing, locating, fixing and retesting a defect.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
A source file is not executed directly. It goes through build stages, after which the program processes actual input.
Distinguish source, compilation, linking and execution.
Read essential diagnostics.
Differentiate syntax, runtime and logic defects.
Support a fix with reproducible tests.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
Source files and builds
C++ is written in text files. A compiler handles source using selected language options, and diagnostic wording varies among tools.
Code Studio's actual capabilities depend on its runtime provider. Do not assume complete C++23 support merely from the tool name.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
Preprocessing, compilation and linking
Preprocessing handles directives such as #include. Compilation checks language constructs and translates code; linking resolves required symbols and libraries.
A missing semicolon typically causes a compilation error; a declared but undefined external function may cause a linker error.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
A program can fail after a successful build
Execution can encounter invalid input, forbidden operations and incorrect decisions. Integer division by zero must be prevented.
With two int operands, 10/3 is 3 rather than 3.333. This is the defined integer operation, not a compiler defect.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
Debugging starts with reproduction
Record the command, input, expected output, actual output and first relevant diagnostic. Classify the phase of failure before editing.
Make one motivated correction and rerun both the failing case and earlier successful cases.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
Standards and portability
Published C++23 is the normative language reference for this curriculum. In October 2026, C++26 remains under development and should not be assumed universally implemented.
The introductory course uses portable fundamentals. STL, exceptions, RAII and build systems require later targeted study and provider verification.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
A minimal reproducible example
A syntax defect prevents a build, for example a missing semicolon. An execution defect or wrong result appears when running: division by zero is invalid, while integer 10/3 yields 3 rather than 3.333. For negative integers, C++ truncates the quotient toward zero: -8/3 is -2. Save source, input, expected and actual output; fix one cause and rerun earlier tests.

records.title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
For the laboratory, a and b are limited to -1000000..1000000 and b must be nonzero. This also excludes quotient overflow.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
RAII: resource management through object initialization and destruction.
Dangling observer: an address or view whose object no longer exists.
unique_ptr: a movable but noncopyable unique object owner.
make_unique: creating an object together with its unique_ptr.
Destructor: a special function invoked at object lifetime end.
move: permitting a move operation rather than copying memory by itself.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
Trace resource creation and destruction and distinguish an owner from a short-lived observer.
Explain: Lifetime and scope
Trace: A minimal constructor vocabulary
Justify: unique_ptr and make_unique
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not generalize unique_ptr emptiness to all moved-from types. Never execute dangling access.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
Lifetime and scope
Scope determines where a name is usable; lifetime determines when its object exists. A local object is normally destroyed on leaving its block, including via return. Copying its address outside does not keep the object alive.
An observer such as int*, a reference, span, or string_view neither releases an object nor extends its owner’s lifetime. Before use, establish that the object is alive and no owner operation has invalidated the address.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
A minimal constructor vocabulary
In struct Trace { explicit Trace(int n):id(n){} ~Trace(){} int id; }; the constructor has the type’s name and no return type. :id(n) initializes the field before the body. ~Trace is called when the object’s lifetime ends.
explicit prevents certain implicit conversions from a single argument. Here the structure is a small explained lifetime-log scaffold; the full treatment of encapsulation and special member functions remains in Module 5.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
RAII binds a resource to an object
RAII means an object acquires a resource during initialization and releases it in its destructor. vector manages a buffer, string manages text, and ofstream will later manage a file. Normal scope exit automatically triggers cleanup.
This is useful even without exceptions. It does not promise destructors will run after process termination or forced Worker cancellation. Saving a learner project and confirming a write are therefore separate interface actions.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
unique_ptr and make_unique
std::unique_ptr<T> from <memory> owns one T object; std::make_unique<T>(args) creates it and returns its owner. An empty pointer is false in a condition. p->value accesses the object’s field, while p.get() obtains a non-owning raw pointer.
Do not delete p.get() or create another owner from the same address. reset() without an argument releases the current object and empties the pointer. Any observers of that released object are then invalid.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
Transferring ownership with move
std::move from <utility> permits a move; the call alone neither relocates memory nor destroys the object. auto q=std::move(p) move-constructs the unique_ptr: q becomes the owner and p becomes empty. Copying a unique_ptr is forbidden.
The T object retains its address during this ownership transfer. An observer remains usable while q owns the live object, but not after q.reset(). Other moved-from types are not necessarily empty unless their documentation promises it.

records.title: Lifetime, RAII, and unique ownership
records.text:
Safe experiments
A log prints create and destroy events; nested blocks reveal reverse destruction order for local objects. Check event counts and owner emptiness after moving rather than dereferencing a released address for an interesting output.
The lab bounds the number of objects and gives each exactly one owner. Draw separate ownership and observation arrows. This will support a small linked list; shared_ptr, the Rule of Five, and deliberate undefined behaviour are not prerequisites here.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Node: a value together with a link to the next structural element.
Head: the owner of the first node or an empty list.
next: an owning successor link in this model.
pushFront: inserting a new node before the former head.
Node observer: a non-owning address used for a short traversal.
Iterative cleanup: destroying nodes successively without a deep call chain.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Build a small singly linked list using unique_ptr and justify each ownership transfer.
Explain: A node and the head
Trace: Insertion at the front
Justify: Iterative cleanup
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not lose the tail when removing the head. Do not generalize O(1) link changes to position lookup.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
A node and the head
Node stores value and unique_ptr<Node> next. head owns the first node, and each next owns its successor. An empty head means an empty list. A valid model has neither ownership cycles nor a second owner of any node.
The ownership lesson introduced explicit Node(int v):value(v){} and ->. A raw Node* is only a traversal observer. It does not delete a node and must not outlive an update that destroys that node.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Insertion at the front
Create a new unique_ptr, move head into newNode->next, then move newNode into head. Every node retains one owner at each step. unique_ptr copying is forbidden and must not be replaced with a copied raw address.
Pushing 1,2,3 at the front yields 3,2,1. That order follows from the operation, not a printing defect. To preserve input order, use a tail-insertion invariant or an appropriate standard container.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Removal without losing ownership
To remove the head, first move head->next into a temporary next, then replace head with next. The old node is destroyed while the tail retains an owner. Check head first: -> through nullptr is invalid.
Do not use an observer of a removed node afterward. A before-and-after diagram is more useful than executing a dangling pointer. Removing an interior node requires the owning link; its value alone is insufficient when duplicates exist.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Iterative cleanup
A unique_ptr chain may be destroyed recursively through next destructors. Huge lists can therefore have depth problems. This lesson bounds the count to 100 and also demonstrates iterative cleanup by detaching next before destroying the head.
while(head) detaches the tail into a temporary owner and replaces the head. Each step destroys exactly one node. Afterward head is empty and observers are no longer used. No shared_ptr or manual delete is required.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Cost depends on the operation
Front insertion and head removal perform O(1) link changes. Searching by value is O(n). An O(1) removal claim assumes the required owning link is already known; locating that position may cost O(n).
vector stores elements compactly, while a list allocates nodes separately and stores links. vector is often simpler for an ordinary catalogue. The teaching list develops ownership reasoning; it is not automatically the right final-project container.

records.title: Linked lists: node invariants and ownership
records.text:
Structural tests
Test empty, singleton, and three-node lists with duplicates, head removal, and complete cleanup. A live-node counter in the extra scaffold should return to zero. A value sum checks data but does not establish every link’s correctness.
Preserve traversal order, node counts, and before-and-after ownership diagrams. Next, stack and queue adapters provide LIFO or FIFO without manually linking nodes and combine queued commands with undo in the project.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
TU: a source file after includes and directives are processed.
Linking: combining compiled parts and resolving external names.
Declaration: describing a name and type without necessarily supplying a body.
Definition: supplying an implementation or object under language rules.
Header guard: preventing repeated inclusion within one TU.
ODR: rules for definition uniqueness and consistency.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
Separate interface and implementation, building the application and test driver as distinct programs.
Explain: Declaration and definition
Trace: A translation unit
Justify: ODR and linking
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not include .cpp files or link two mains together. A header guard is not a program-wide definition registry.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
Declaration and definition
int twice(int); declares the name, parameter, and result without a body. int twice(int x){return 2*x;} defines the function. A caller needs a compatible declaration, and the final program needs the corresponding definition.
domain.hpp holds the shared interface, domain.cpp includes it and supplies the body, and main.cpp includes it and calls the function. The compiler can then check implementation against interface rather than trusting manually repeated signatures.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
A translation unit
After #include processing, a .cpp and its included headers form a translation unit, or TU. Compile each .cpp separately. A header is normally not a standalone build unit, and a .cpp should not be included into another .cpp.
includeRoots specifies directories for user headers. With include/domain.hpp and #include "domain.hpp", add include. translationUnits lists main.cpp and src/domain.cpp. File paths belong to the project, not to absolute machine locations.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
Header guards
An #ifndef DOMAIN_HPP / #define DOMAIN_HPP / #endif guard prevents repeated inclusion within one TU. Use a unique guard name. It prevents repeated structure definitions within a TU, not multiple ordinary function definitions across a program.
A header should include the standard headers it needs. Do not depend on accidental include order in main.cpp. Avoid using namespace std in a public header because it changes every including file’s environment.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
ODR and linking
The One Definition Rule requires consistent definitions; an ordinary external function needs one definition in the program. Placing its body in a header included by two .cpp files may cause multiple definition at linking. inline has special rules and is not an arbitrary patch.
If the declaration is visible but domain.cpp is absent from the build, the caller may compile and then fail linking with an unresolved symbol. Distinguish that from an unknown-name compile error. The lesson includes intentional negative controls.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
Build the application and tests separately
The application has one main in main.cpp and the test driver another in tests.cpp. Do not link both together. Build the application from main.cpp and domain.cpp, and tests from tests.cpp and domain.cpp using separate translationUnits lists.
Create files through Code Studio and select the intended entry. If a project automatically builds every .cpp, keep the driver in a separate project or explicitly exclude it from that build. Never rename personal source files without preserving a copy.

records.title: Multifile builds: headers, translation units, and ODR
records.text:
A reproducible build
Preserve file paths, includeRoots, translationUnits, and the C++20 standard. A desktop compiler uses the equivalent -Iinclude main.cpp src/domain.cpp principle. Instructions must not contain another machine’s private paths or secrets.
Check a successful build, a missing definition, a duplicate definition, and recovery after correction. Compare stdout and exit code. File import requires similar precision next: a filename alone does not prove persistence between runs.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Logical length: the number of elements belonging to the data.
Stable filtering: preserving selected elements’ relative order.
Index: an element position in [0,size).
Duplicate: a repeated value at another position.
Linear search: checking successive elements until a match or the end.
End position: a completion marker, not an accessible element.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Connect every index to a valid range and distinguish storage capacity from logical length.
Explain: The object and its elements
Trace: Arrays in parameters
Justify: Stable filtering
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not initialize a minimum from a[0] before checking nonemptiness. Do not use a VLA as standard C++20.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
The object and its elements
int values[4]{} creates four zero-initialized ints with indices 0,1,2,3. Four is the count, not the final index. A built-in array’s bound in ordinary C++ must be a constant expression; int a[n] with a runtime n is not a standard solution.
Use vector for a changing size, or a fixed buffer with a separate count<=capacity. {} initialization never permits access beyond the array. All buffer elements exist, but only the first count may represent task data.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Arrays in parameters
An int a[] parameter is adjusted to int*, so the declaration does not carry the length into the function. sizeof that parameter measures a pointer. Do not derive length using sizeof(a)/sizeof(a[0]) inside such a function.
Pass span<const int> or an explicit pointer/length pair with a proven contract. Here span preserves bounds. At the actual array declaration, sizeof applies to the array, but a clear interface remains preferable.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Linear search
Search left to right, comparing each element with the target. Return the first matching index. If none matches, return a separate flag or size() as an end position; callers must check that result before indexing.
An empty range has no match. Duplicates require a policy: first, last, or all indices. The lab counts qualifying elements, so each visited index contributes once even when values repeat.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Stable filtering
To select nonnegative values, traverse the input and append qualifying values to a new vector. Relative order is preserved, and an empty result is valid. Sum only selected values; do not confuse an element count with a sum of indices.
In-place filtering can use a write index with write<=read: read the original element before writing a selected one. That requires another invariant. Begin with two containers so memory optimization does not obscure correctness.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Minimum and empty input
An empty range has no minimum. Do not initialize the minimum to zero when all values may be positive. After checking nonemptiness, start with the first element and compare the rest; a later structure can carry an explicit presence flag.
For n<=100 and |value|<=1000, the absolute sum is at most 100000. For a[i], establish both i<count and count<=capacity. The compiler is not required to diagnose a violation.

records.title: One-dimensional arrays: indexing, filtering, and search
records.text:
Comparing representations
The same span-based algorithm should return identical results for int[], array, and vector. Ownership, resizing, and interfaces differ, not the sequence’s mathematical meaning. Avoid coupling a computation to a global buffer.
Test an empty set, one negative value, one zero, all selected, none selected, and duplicates. Record expected order and count for each. Next, add a second coordinate while explicitly checking matrix shape.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Object: Storage with a type and lifetime; it need not be an instance of a user-defined class.
Abstraction: Selected observable properties that hide decisions a client does not need.
Invariant: A condition established at construction and preserved by public operations.
Contract: Conditions governing valid calls, results, effects and rejection.
State: Values that determine an object's subsequent observable behaviour.
Member function: A function member invoked on a selected object.
Responsibility: A coherent task assigned to a type and a reason for changing its code.
Instance: A particular object of a type with its own state.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Build a domain model and explain why its operations preserve an invariant.
Separate Counter fields from operations.
Trace 30,80,20 without running.
Justify checking before adding.
Test independence of two Counters.
Compare an open record with a class for this task.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
From a record to a domain object
In Module 3 a structure grouped related data, such as a sensor reading and its unit. In the language an object has storage, a type and a lifetime; an int variable is an object too. Design uses a more specific idea: a representation of a domain concept together with the operations allowed on it.
Not every record needs a hierarchy. If every combination of fields is meaningful, a plain struct with public data and free functions can be clearer. When values must satisfy a relationship, such as a counter remaining between zero and one hundred, the type should control changes. Begin with that requirement rather than with class syntax.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Reading a first class
In Counter the name after class declares a new type. The value_ field belongs separately to each instance, and =0 supplies its initial value. Members before public: are private in a class. Members after public: form operations callers can use. The semicolon following the closing brace completes the class declaration.
Counter a,b creates two independent objects. Calling a.add(7) selects a, so value_ inside the method denotes a's field. The value() const method observes state; const prevents ordinary modification of fields through this object. Constructors receive their own lesson. For now, a field initializer and the automatically generated constructor establish the starting state.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Invariant and operation contract
An invariant is a statement that holds after construction and after every public operation finishes. Counter promises a value between zero and one hundred. The add contract accepts only a nonnegative increment that fits the remaining capacity. Success returns true; rejection returns false and preserves the previous value. These are observable promises that tests can check.
The n>100-value_ check happens before addition. Testing value_+n>100 is less safe because a sufficiently large n could overflow int before comparison. Here the remaining capacity stays within zero to one hundred, and the first condition rejects negative increments. The pre-call invariant and these checks justify the post-call invariant, beyond a single successful demonstration.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Abstraction hides decisions
A caller needs add and value, rather than the spelling or representation of a private field. The representation can later change while the contract remains stable. Abstraction selects the observable properties needed for a task. This reduces the number of details a reader must hold in mind when checking a program.
Hiding a field alone does not create a useful interface. Unrestricted getValue/setValue operations can still violate the meaning of a type. Names such as reserve, ship or accept express intent and conditions better than a universal setter. Conversely, a simple immutable record should not acquire methods merely to look object oriented.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Responsibility and dependencies
The counter is responsible for a valid value, not for reading cin, selecting a UI language or saving a project. Separation lets you test an object without a browser or a file. The application parses input first, invokes domain operations second and formats output last. Each part has a distinct reason to change.
Do not move every function into a giant Application class. Examine responsibilities by asking which requirement would force this code to change. A new input format should not require changing counter arithmetic. Collaboration between small types is often more useful than a deep hierarchy; inheritance comes after ownership and contracts in this module.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Testing two objects
In the worked example a accepts seven, then rejects ninety-four, while b remains zero. The output is 7 0 0: the first state, the second state and the last success flag. That final zero does not indicate a damaged object. Rejection is an expected operation result, distinct from a malformed input stream.
An independent test should modify only a and observe b. It catches an accidentally shared static field. Also test repeated rejection, a zero increment and filling exactly to capacity. Compare state before and after a rejected call. Checking only the returned bool misses an implementation that changes a field before returning false.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Laboratory protocol
The laboratory reads an operation count from zero to twenty and exactly that many integer increments. It validates all input syntax before producing a domain result. An increment such as minus one or one hundred and one is a domain rejection and increases rejected. An unknown token or a missing number makes the entire input invalid.
For three increments 30 80 20, the state trace is zero, thirty, thirty, fifty, with one rejection. Write that trace before running the program. Test the maximum int separately: the contract rejects it without overflowing. The supplied cases are checkable examples; add an independent case and an invariant explanation rather than relying solely on matching stdout.

records.title: Objects, abstraction and responsibility boundaries
records.text:
Choosing a model
Compare two solutions to the same task: an open structure with a validation function, and a class with private state. Identify places where the first permits a forgotten check and describe the extra code required by the second. Choose object oriented design for manageable dependencies and invariants, rather than assuming every free function needs a class.
During review explain who owns state, who can change it and what a test observes. These runs do not establish safety for arbitrary programs. They support a contract for a bounded model and specific checked cases. The next lesson develops interfaces with related fields, const correctness and operations that preserve several conditions together.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
Reference T&: In our declarations, an alias of an existing object; it needs initialization and cannot be reseated.
Pointer T*: A separate object holding a pointer value, such as the address of a suitable live T or nullptr.
Address-of &: In &value, produces a pointer to the value object.
Indirection *: In *pointer, refers to the pointed-to object; access needs a valid pointer and valid lifetime.
nullptr: A null pointer value; it must not be dereferenced.
Dangling pointer: A pointer whose former object has ended its lifetime; being non-null does not prove safe access.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
Trace a live object through several access paths and distinguish changing an address from changing a value.
Distinguish a value copy, reference, and pointer.
Read T&, T*, &object, and *pointer in context.
Check nullptr before access and account for lifetime.
Explain read-only access through const int* and const int&.
Draw symbolic links without relying on actual addresses.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
Session 1. Three relationships to a value
After int value{10};, int copy = value; creates an independent int. int& alias = value; creates a reference to the original object: alias is another way to refer to value, not a snapshot. alias = 12; changes value. Contrast this with lesson 5 copying.
In a declaration, & beside a type introduces a reference. In int* pointer = &value;, * beside the type declares a pointer and &value on the right obtains an address. Symbols have different roles in declarations and expressions; read the complete construct.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
A pointer is separate; an address is not a stock value
pointer holds a pointer value, while *pointer refers to the target object. *pointer = 15; changes value. pointer = &second; changes the pointer itself so access now leads to second. These are different operations and different state-journal events.
A diagram may name objects A and B and draw pointer → A. These are symbolic labels rather than numeric addresses. Actual addresses depend on the run, target, and environment and must not become expected stdout or stable learning-object identifiers.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
A reference is not reseated
After int& alias = first;, alias = second; copies second’s current value into first rather than switching the reference. selected = &second; really does reseat a pointer. Observe both original objects when testing or the distinction can remain invisible.
A reference is useful when access consistently names a known live object. A pointer can represent absence or selection, but does not by itself mean ownership. Neither references nor pointers here create or delete their targets.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
Session 2. nullptr and lifetime
int* selected{nullptr}; explicitly means no selected object. Check selected != nullptr before reading *selected. The familiar if/else chooses a safe branch: absent when null, or the value when present. This checks absence rather than proving every aspect of pointer validity.
A non-null pointer can dangle after its target leaves an inner block. Checking nullptr does not extend lifetime. Every dereference here targets a live object; null and dangling pointers are never dereferenced, even as a bad experiment. Record that data outlive all access paths in your project.

records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
const restricts a particular access path
const int* observer = &value; permits reading *observer but not changing value through this pointer. The original value can remain an ordinary int: value = 14; is valid and the observer sees 14. Likewise const int& view prohibits mutation through view. Read-only access does not imply that the source object can never change.
Do not remove const through a guessed cast to silence a diagnostic. The negative example deliberately requires a build rejection when writing through const int*. A constant pointer itself, int* const, can be studied later; the introductory contract focuses on const before int.
