records.title: Objects, copies, references, and pointers: links without unsafe memory
records.text:
An object journal and checks
In the laboratory, stock and snapshot are two objects; selectedStock references stock and stockPointer points to it. Subtracting 3 through the reference and adding 2 through the pointer gives 9 while the snapshot remains 10. Do not invent a separate stored-value object for selectedStock; the reference accesses stock.
Repeat the operations from initial values 3 and 20, safely within range. Explain the null example separately without forcing a crash. Preserve both a legend-labeled diagram and stdout: a picture alone does not prove execution, and stdout alone does not explain object relationships.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
Input: Data supplied for a particular execution of a program.
Precondition: A constraint under which the requested behavior is defined.
Test case: A concrete input together with the expected observable result.
Compiler: A tool that checks and translates C++ source for the build process.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
A program is a testable model of a problem, not merely a collection of commands. Start with inputs, rules and observable results.
Distinguish the problem statement, algorithm, implementation and tests.
Specify inputs, outputs and boundary cases.
Explain why a successful build does not establish correctness.
Change a program and demonstrate the effect with reproducible tests.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
Agree on behavior before writing code
To compute the total for a shopping basket, we need a unit price, quantity and a rule: price multiplied by quantity. The requirement is incomplete until invalid inputs and numeric bounds have been discussed.
A table of cases makes expectations explicit: 120 and 3 must yield 360; 120 and 0 must yield 0; a negative price must be rejected or handled under an agreed policy.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
An algorithm bridges a requirement and a programming language
An algorithm specifies the necessary steps: read values, check them, compute a result and produce output. It can be expressed without using C++ syntax at all.
The same steps can be implemented in different languages. The required outcome remains the benchmark against which each implementation is evaluated.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
What happens when C++ is executed
A developer edits source files; compilation checks the language rules and translates source; linking assembles required components; execution runs the program. A failure can occur at different stages.
A program using addition instead of multiplication might compile and run without any warning. It is still wrong for this requirement. Debugging means reproducing the mismatch, locating its cause and retesting.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
Tests are evidence, not decoration
A test case states input, expected output and observed output. Running the same case after a change is regression testing: it checks that a fix did not break behavior that used to work.
Use ordinary, boundary and invalid inputs. A single successful run says very little about the full input space or the quality of a program.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
A disciplined development cycle
Clarify the problem, model the data, design an algorithm, implement it, run checks, explain results and refine. This ordering reduces random code changes.
Document the accepted inputs, error policy and outputs in words another person can understand. These notes are part of an engineering deliverable.

records.title: How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
How programming works: from a real problem to a verified solution
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
Price and quantity are integers 0..1000; discount is 0..100. Round the saving down to whole units: total = subtotal − (subtotal·discount)/100. The bounds keep intermediate products within a 32-bit int.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Property: A statement about a class of inputs, such as multiset preservation.
Oracle: An independent way to obtain the expected result.
Metamorphic relation: A relation between results on transformed inputs when the full answer is unknown.
Mutation: A controlled change to a correct program to evaluate tests.
steady_clock: A monotonic clock suitable for interval measurements.
Warmup: An unrecorded preliminary run under an explicit policy.
Sample: Individual observations retained before computing summaries.
Conclusion validity: Matching the scope of a claim to the experiment actually performed.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Combine an independent oracle, metamorphic properties, a safe mutation and a reproducible measurement log.
Combine examples, properties and an independent oracle.
Detect a safe logical mutation.
Separate data preparation from the measured region.
Preserve repeated raw measurements with units.
Limit performance conclusions to the actual protocol.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Examples, properties and proofs
An example connects one input to an expected output. A property describes a class of inputs, such as sorted output preserving the input multiset. A proof explains why the algorithm satisfies the condition over its valid modeled domain. These forms of evidence complement one another; a passing test does not turn into a proof.
Start with independent small expectations: [3,1,3] must become [1,3,3], not [1,3]. Add general properties next. They can detect failures on unfamiliar data, but the properties themselves need scrutiny. For record sorting, keys alone are insufficient: check IDs and associated fields, using original labels to check stability.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Oracles and independence
An oracle supplies an expected answer. It can be a linear scan for search, a hand-built table for small inputs, or a library sort plus multiset checks for an educational sort. Two copies of one function are not independent oracles. State the assumptions behind your chosen method.
Test properties against known-bad outputs too. An all-zero array may be ordered but lose the input; a reversed array can preserve multiplicities while violating order. Such negative controls show that the checker distinguishes substantive defects rather than always returning true.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Metamorphic relations
When a large exact answer is inconvenient, relate several runs. Sorting an already sorted integer result should not change it: idempotence. A permutation or reversal of the input should sort to the same value array. Doubling each permitted integer preserves relative order provided arithmetic does not overflow.
A relation must fit the contract. Permuting input records can change the tied-label order of a stable sort, so entire-record output equality need not hold. Shifting all search keys requires shifting the target too. Justify the relation first, then test it under explicit arithmetic bounds.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Generation, shrinking and safe mutation
Combine fixed input classes with several saved seeds. Shrink a failing case by removing items or simplifying values while preserving failure, then keep the minimal case in regression. An extension exhaustively enumerates lengths up to six over {-1,0,1}: 1093 collections, not every input in the general domain.
A mutation is a small intentional implementation change that a test should detect. The example truncates a pass while keeping every index valid. Success means detecting the defect, not the mutant working correctly. Do not use an invalid std::sort comparator, out-of-bounds access or signed overflow as the mutation; a defined but wrong result is sufficient.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Which clock and which region?
Use std::chrono::steady_clock for durations: its readings do not move backward as time progresses. end−start is a duration; duration_cast converts units. elapsed_ns names nanoseconds as a unit, not a promise of nanosecond resolution or accuracy. A very short measured interval may legitimately produce zero.
Copy input before start, then validate and write files after end. The measured region is the selected sort, not the whole process. C++ compilation, compiler download, UI and Worker startup are separate costs. End-to-end user latency needs another protocol, which this lab does not perform.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Warmup, repeats and uncontrolled factors
Before five recorded runs per algorithm, the lab performs one unrecorded warmup pass. Every run receives a fresh copy of base; otherwise insertion would see already sorted input after the first run. Validate every result so a fast wrong answer cannot enter the comparison table as an achievement.
The teaching code runs std_sort before insertion, which can itself introduce order bias. Browser load, scheduling, caches and compiler settings also affect observations. A serious comparison needs more sizes and input classes, run-order control, more repeats and environment details. Do not label this small protocol an already completed research benchmark.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
Raw samples and an honest conclusion
timings.tsv has ten rows after the header: algorithm, iteration, elapsed_ns. Check five distinct iterations 0…4 per algorithm and nonnegative integer durations. Native and WASI timing numbers are not required to match exactly. Retain all samples instead of only the most flattering minimum.
Median and spread help describe observations, but five values at one size give a limited picture. State size, data class, preparation and the exact timed region. Say so if differences are comparable to noise. O(n²) versus O(n log n) follows from models and growth reasoning; seconds can investigate a practical hypothesis without supplying that foundation.

records.title: Property checking and honest experiments
records.text:
The final project and its defence
The project connects eight topics: catalogue validation, ID/value indexes, stable recursive merging, binary boundaries, frequencies and an RNG audit. Its report has deterministic ordering. A separate driver checks functions; the separate lab supplies raw timings. Do not link two mains or confuse saving an artifact with an automatic Cloud push.
In the defence, explain an index invariant, preparation/query costs, rejection without a partial report and a counterexample to a wrong solution. Then implement a small requirement with independent tests. Public cases and references support learning rather than a protected examination service; completed flags and passing runs do not automatically create mastery or a university grade.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Engine: A deterministic state machine producing a sequence.
Seed: An initial value for generator state initialization.
Distribution: Transforming random bits into values with a chosen distribution.
mt19937: A standardized generator with a specified raw-output algorithm.
Modulo bias: Unequal preimage counts when target size does not divide source size.
Repeatability: Matching results with the same environment, initial state and call history.
Uniformity: Equal modeled probabilities, not equal frequencies in every small sample.
Noncryptographic: Unsuitable for secrets or adversarial prediction resistance.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Separate engines, distributions, seeds and saved datasets; test promised properties without inventing guarantees.
Separate engine from distribution.
Validate the seed domain before conversion.
Explain modulo bias.
Test repeatability with identical state histories.
Preserve experiment data and parameters.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
A deterministic sequence and state
A pseudorandom engine computes an output from its state and updates that state. Equal initial states and equal call histories produce equal streams. The output may look random without being physical randomness. An extra call, even for debugging output, shifts all later values.
A seed initializes state under the engine’s rules. Copying an engine copies state rather than magically creating an independent source. Recreating an engine from the same seed at every step restarts its sequence. Create one engine for a series and explicitly define where a new reproducible experiment begins.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
A named engine versus a library choice
std::mt19937 has standard-specified parameters, and C++20 specifies a check value for its default-constructed engine’s 10000th output. This enables an exact cross-environment check of that stream. default_random_engine is an implementation choice, so sharing its type name does not prove two platforms use the same algorithm.
Exactly 10000 calls in the worked example yield 4123659995. This is a narrow assertion about that engine, not every <random> generator. Do not transfer that precision to mapping into a desired range: a distribution is a separate step with its own contract and potentially its own state.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
A distribution specifies a law and range
uniform_int_distribution<int>(lo,hi) produces uniform integers over a closed range, including both endpoints. Check lo≤hi before constructing it. The lab bounds endpoints to −1000…1000 to avoid relying on int extremes. lo==hi is valid: every result is the range’s single value.
The algorithm mapping engine outputs to a distribution can differ between standard libraries. The same mt19937 and seed therefore need not yield the same distributed array on libc++ and libstdc++. This lesson checks range, length and replay within one implementation; cross-environment defect replay uses the saved actual-number file.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Why a remainder can introduce bias
Imagine a uniform source over 0…7 and a desired output over 0…2. Remainder modulo three gives three preimages each for zero and one, but only two for two. The output is therefore biased despite the uniform source. A small sample can accidentally hide this structural bias.
Discarding six and seven before taking the remainder leaves two preimages per result in this toy model. That explains rejection sampling without directing you to implement a production distribution. A standard distribution expresses the intent more clearly, but still needs valid bounds and a reproducibility policy.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Replay is a controlled experiment
The lab creates two engines with one seed and two distributions with matching parameters, then makes the same calls in the same order. The arrays must match within the current implementation. Save samples.txt, repeat.txt, compiler/runtime and parameters. Do not infer replay solely from a printed “yes”; compare the actual files.
Different seeds need not produce different observed arrays: n=0 makes both empty, lo==hi makes every value identical, and short samples can coincide too. A mandatory “different seeds, different arrays” test would invent a guarantee. List the promised properties before testing plausible-sounding assumptions.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Properties, frequencies and false conclusions
Check exact length, each value’s bounds and replay of the corresponding runs. all_of is true on an empty range, so verify length separately. These checks do not prove uniformity: always printing lo can satisfy them. Explaining the actual distribution choice and inspecting source are part of the manual rubric.
A histogram helps explore data, but a uniform law does not require perfectly equal counts in every finite sample. A statistical test needs a hypothesis, sample size and false-positive policy. This lesson does not substitute an arbitrary threshold; it checks deterministic contract properties and preserves observations.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Test generation and security boundaries
Random cases supplement empty, minimum, maximum, all-equal and already ordered inputs rather than replacing them. Save the seed of a discovered failure, then shrink the actual data to a comprehensible counterexample. A small fixed regression case is usually more useful than hoping to rediscover the defect randomly.
mt19937 is not intended for cryptographic tasks. This browser runtime does not treat random_device as a guaranteed system-entropy source. Do not use the educational generator for security-critical values. Sampling without replacement and shuffling have their own contracts; sorting with a “random comparator” is not a safe substitute because it violates ordering requirements.

records.title: Pseudorandomness and reproducibility
records.text:
Lab artifacts and the next experiment
Before running, record n, seed, endpoints and expected logical results. Afterward check both file shapes, line counts, bounds and equality. Keep source and environment details. Across native and WASI, compare the promised properties; different raw distributed numbers alone are not a runtime defect.
The next lesson uses fixed data to compare algorithms and separate clocks to observe cost. Saved inputs let you separate computation differences from generation differences. Input class, program version, verification method and raw samples become part of a reproducible engineering experiment.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
GCD: The greatest positive integer dividing both inputs without a remainder.
Remainder: For nonnegative a and positive b, a%b is between 0 and b-1.
GCD invariant: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,a mod b), provided b>0.
Trace: A sequence of intermediate states such as a,b and remainder.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Instead of guessing a greatest common divisor, we repeatedly transform a pair of integers without changing the answer.
Trace the greatest common divisor calculation by hand.
Explain (a,b) → (b,a mod b).
Identify the invariant and termination argument.
Test the implementation with normal and boundary cases.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Why remainders make the problem smaller
We could try every possible divisor of 48 and 18, but division tells us that 48 = 2×18 + 12. Any common divisor of 48 and 18 must also divide 12.
Therefore gcd(48,18) equals gcd(18,12), then gcd(12,6), then gcd(6,0). The result is 6. Each transformation preserves the sought divisor.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Pseudocode and state transitions
Start with (a,b). While b is not zero, compute r=a mod b, then replace a with b and b with r. The remainder is never computed with divisor zero.
For 48 and 18, the trace reads (48,18,12) → (18,12,6) → (12,6,0) → (6,0). The second component decreases after each iteration.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Why the GCD invariant holds
If a number divides both a and b, it also divides a-qb and thus the remainder r. Conversely, a common divisor of b and r divides a=qb+r.
The two pairs have the same common divisors. Once b=0, the current a is the GCD for the stated valid input domain.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Why the loop must stop
For nonnegative a and positive b, the remainder is nonnegative and strictly smaller than b. The second component cannot keep decreasing forever without reaching zero.
Inputs (0,18) and (18,0) both have GCD 18. In this teaching contract (0,0) is rejected explicitly because it has no unique greatest positive divisor.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Build a safe C++ implementation
Read and validate inputs before the loop. We accept nonnegative values within int range, excluding (0,0). Production-grade code also needs bounds and input-failure handling.
To debug, compare the full trace, not only the last output. Calculate the remainder before overwriting the previous pair.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Why the pair replacement preserves the GCD
If a = q·b + r, every common divisor of a and b divides r = a − q·b. Conversely, a common divisor of b and r divides a. Thus the common divisors are unchanged. With b>0, 0≤r<b, so the second value strictly decreases to zero. These arguments establish answer preservation and termination separately. For (18,48), the first remainder is 18; reversed inputs still work.

records.title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
Laboratory inputs are a,b from 0 to 100000, excluding (0,0). These bounds match the interactive model.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
RAII: Tying resource ownership to the lifetime of an owning object.
Unique pointer: A movable, noncopyable exclusive owner.
Make unique: Construction that immediately places an object under a unique_ptr.
Borrowing: Observing an object while ownership remains elsewhere.
Shared pointer: Shared ownership managed through a common control block.
Weak pointer: A nonowning link to an object under shared ownership.
Lock: Obtaining a temporary strong owner if the object still exists.
Rule of zero: Relying on owning members rather than manual special-member operations.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Separate ownership from observation and check early-exit cleanup and a weak back-reference.
Draw ownership and observation arrows.
Predict both exits from work.
Check weak_ptr before and after reset.
Remove unnecessary shared ownership from a parameter.
Design a tree with a back-reference.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
A resource is more than memory
A resource may be memory, a file, a lock or a registered action. Each has acquisition and release operations. Manual cleanup at the bottom of a function is fragile because an early return introduces an easily missed path. RAII connects ownership to an object's lifetime and makes cleanup follow scope exit.
The teaching Resource increments an external counter and decrements it in its destructor. std::make_unique creates an owner whose destructor deletes Resource. When work returns early, the local unique_ptr is still destroyed. This demonstrates ordinary early exit; cleanup during exception propagation is checked separately in the exception lesson.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Exclusive ownership
unique_ptr<T> represents the sole owner of a dynamically allocated T. It cannot be copied, but ownership can be transferred by moving. make_unique<T>(args) constructs an object and immediately places it under an owner. get() returns an observing raw pointer; it neither transfers ownership nor permits the caller to delete it.
Dereferencing *p or using p->member requires a nonnull pointer. After reset the previous object is destroyed and its observers are invalid. Never build another unique_ptr from p.get(): that would create two owners and cause repeated deletion. The negative example rejects copying at compile time, before any execution can occur.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Observers and borrowing
A T& reference or T* pointer often borrows an object owned elsewhere. Identify the owner and the period during which the observer is valid. Passing Resource& to a function that does not retain it bounds the borrowing to that call. Storing a raw pointer in a longer-lived object requires an additional lifetime contract.
Do not replace every pointer with shared_ptr to create an appearance of safety. Ownership should express an architectural decision rather than copying convenience. When data fits directly in a vector or another object's field, separate allocation may be unnecessary. Start with values and justify the need for a dynamic lifetime.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Shared ownership and its cost
shared_ptr supports multiple owners through a shared control block. Copying it increases the owner count, and destroying the last owner releases the object. The control block and counter updates have costs, so this is not a free universal pointer. Ownership accounting does not synchronize access to the pointed-to object's state.
make_shared is usually clearer than combining new and shared_ptr manually. Shared ownership should still answer a domain question: why should several independent components determine this object's lifetime? If the answer is merely easier parameter passing, consider a const reference. use_count is not a reliable protocol for exclusive access in concurrent code.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Cycles and weak_ptr
When a parent owns a child through shared_ptr and the child strongly owns the parent, both counts may remain nonzero indefinitely. weak_ptr observes a control block without extending the object's lifetime. A back-reference to the parent is therefore often weak, preserving a clear direction of ownership.
lock() obtains a temporary shared_ptr if the object still exists, or returns an empty one otherwise. Acquire the lock first and use its result within that owner's lifetime. In the example observed is destroyed before root.reset(), so the weak pointer is expired afterwards. Destruction cannot be expected while a local strong owner remains alive.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
The rule of zero
Members such as vector, string and unique_ptr release their own resources. A class containing them often needs no user-written destructor or special copy and move functions. This is the rule of zero. It reduces the amount of code that must manually coordinate ownership across ordinary and exceptional paths.
The rule of zero does not promise that every such class is copyable. A unique_ptr member disables implicit copying, whereas string and vector usually provide value semantics. That difference is useful. Select member types with suitable contracts, then check which operations the composed type actually supports. The next lesson organizes copy and move semantics.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Laboratory: early exits
With n zero, work creates one owner and returns immediately; the final output must be active 0. With n one, two owners exist and the function prints two before returning, followed by active 0. The counter is declared in main and outlives the owners, making observation after work valid.
Extend the test with another early return after the second acquisition and predict active first. Do not add an exception before studying that separate contract. Document each path: acquired resources, responsible owners and resources left afterwards. These checked paths do not establish the absence of every possible leak in a future application.

records.title: RAII and smart pointers
records.text:
Reviewing an ownership choice
Draw an object graph with separate owns and observes arrows. Give each arrow a lifetime boundary. If strong ownership forms a cycle, identify who breaks it or replace a justified back-reference with weak_ptr. A weak reference is especially useful when disappearance of the target is an acceptable state.
Check for manual deletion of get(), duplicate owners of one address and dereferencing empty pointers. Compare the design with storing a value directly in a container. A successful design often uses fewer pointers rather than more. You can now examine transferring owners between objects without losing responsibility for cleanup.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Base case: A simple case that ends a branch without another call.
Measure: A nonnegative quantity decreasing strictly before a recursive step.
Call frame: Separate parameters and local objects for one invocation.
Depth: The maximum simultaneously active calls along one branch.
Divide: Splitting a problem into smaller subproblems.
Conquer: Solving subproblems under their contracts.
Merge: Combining two ordered ranges in linear work.
Recurrence: Relating problem cost to subproblem and combination costs.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Prove the base case is reachable, trace returns and construct a stable merge over bounded input.
Prove termination with a decreasing measure.
Trace calls and returns.
Implement stable merging.
Derive a merge-sort recurrence.
Separate stack depth and buffer size.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
A call preserves a continuation
A recursive function calls itself directly or through other functions. Each call has its own parameters and local objects. In factorial(4), 4·factorial(3) remains unfinished until the inner result returns. A trace must therefore show both descent 4→3→2→1 and return values 1→2→6→24.
A conventional implementation stores continuation state on a call stack. This is not the std::stack container from the previous module: calls are managed by the language/runtime, while the container holds application data. Never return a reference to a local object whose call has ended. Mutate a live external vector through a reference and pass subproblem bounds as values.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
A base case and a progress measure
A base case produces its answer without another recursive call. Factorial returns one at zero and one. A sort needs no work on a range shorter than two. Handle the base case before operations requiring an element: an empty range has no a[0], though sorting it is valid.
The progress measure must strictly decrease within a well-founded domain. For factorial(n−1) at n≥2 it is n; for merge sort it is hi−lo. Checking n<0 before conversion to unsigned is essential, or a negative input becomes a large positive value and changes the argument. “It will stop eventually” is not a named progress measure.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Induction connects a local step to the answer
Assume a call correctly solves a smaller problem. Then multiplying n by a correct factorial(n−1) gives factorial(n), provided arithmetic is valid. This is the inductive step; the base case anchors it. Assuming correctness for a problem of the same size is circular and supplies no termination proof.
For merge sort the assumption covers two smaller ranges. After they return, merging still needs its own proof: correct halves do not guarantee the next item is chosen correctly. Separate valid splitting, correct smaller solutions and correct combination preserving every item.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Splitting and the call tree
Use [lo,hi) and mid=lo+(hi−lo)/2. At length at least two, both halves are smaller. Their lengths can differ by one: seven items split into three and four. Draw the size tree 7→(3,4) down to singletons; empty and singleton leaves use the base case.
The lab numbers the root depth as one, including an empty input. maximum is the deepest executed call, not the total number of calls. For 128 items it is eight, following from balanced splitting and that numbering convention. This small experiment does not determine the browser’s maximum stack capacity.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Merging two prepared fronts
After sorting the halves, i and j identify their first unconsumed items. The invariant says tmp holds the smallest items already selected in order, while both remainders remain sorted. Compare their fronts and append the smaller. When one half is exhausted, append the other remainder in its existing order.
Choose the left half on ties when stability is required. The code tests right<left first and otherwise selects left. tmp then has hi−lo items and copies back to the same range. Do not read a[i] at i==mid or a[j] at j==hi; boundary checks precede the comparison.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Recurrence cost and memory
Merging n bounded integers takes linear work. T(n)=T(⌊n/2⌋)+T(⌈n/2⌉)+Θ(n) gives Θ(n log n): each level processes about n items in total and there are about log n levels. This is a level-by-level argument, not a deduction from one timing graph.
Here tmp is created after both child calls return. Peak auxiliary-buffer space is O(n), with O(log n) active call frames. Repeated allocation still affects constants; a shared workspace buffer is a separate design option. Total allocated bytes over a run and maximum simultaneously occupied memory are different metrics.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Depth, repeated work and bounded rejection
Not every recursion is balanced. Splitting n into n−1 and one gives linear depth, while naive Fibonacci repeats identical subproblems many times. Estimate both call count and path depth before choosing recursion. Iteration or an explicit work stack may be preferable when depth follows potentially large input.
The lab rejects n>128 before sorting; the factorial example is limited to 12. These are documented educational bounds, not an ability to process every input. Do not promise tail-call elimination as a required guarantee of ordinary C++ code. Timeouts and stack exhaustion should not be your main precondition checks.

records.title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
records.text:
Traces, tests and transfer
Draw the call tree for n=3, then a return trace showing the halves being merged. Test empty, singleton, odd-length, reverse, duplicate and maximum-size data. Validate maximum under the stated root-depth-one convention. Check multiset preservation separately: a correct depth says nothing about preserved values.
Extend values with original labels and demonstrate stability on tied keys. Compare local and shared-buffer space without calling an assumption a measurement. Next, choose containers for key-based queries; a container’s potentially recursive implementation does not replace understanding its public contract.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
Predicate: Here, a bool expression describing a property to check.
Logical AND: Built-in && is true when both operands are true; the right operand is skipped when the left is false.
Logical OR: Built-in || is true when at least one operand is true; the right operand is skipped when the left is true.
Negation: ! reverses true and false after converting the operand to bool.
Short-circuit evaluation: Skipping the right operand when the left already determines a built-in logical expression’s result.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
Build conditions from clear parts and identify right operands that will not be evaluated.
Read <, <=, >, >=, ==, and != as bool-producing comparisons.
Express a range as two comparisons joined by &&.
Explain &&, ||, ! and selected truth tables.
Place a divisor guard before a dangerous expression.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
A comparison is a value, not assignment
score >= 0 produces bool. == compares equality and != inequality; a single = in assignment changes an object. score = 0 can be valid C++ inside a larger expression, but it is not an equality check. Inspect meaning even after a successful build.
Identify operand types first. As seen previously, int and unsigned int can change the expected meaning of a negative comparison. Our ranges use matching ints so that logic is studied without hidden mixed-sign conversions.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
A range is not a mathematical comparison chain
C++ 0 <= score <= 100 does not express two simultaneous bounds. First 0 <= score produces bool, which is then compared with 100. For the resulting 0 or 1, that second comparison is true even when score is invalid.
Use score >= 0 && score <= 100. One comparison checks the lower bound and one the upper; both must hold. Name the result validScore when useful in the next stage. Bounds are inclusive: 0 and 100 are valid, −1 and 101 are not.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
A truth table without hidden execution
&& is true only for true/true. || is false only for false/false. !true is false. A table of final values does not by itself show which operands were evaluated: built-in && skips the right operand after false, and built-in || skips it after true.
Zero converts to false and a nonzero number to true. Two is not a third logical value. Prefer domain conditions such as connected && !maintenance to unexplained numeric flags.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
Protection depends on the correct order
In divisor != 0 && 12 / divisor > 1 the divisor is checked first. At zero the left side is false, so division is skipped. Reversing the operands breaks protection by attempting division first. We discuss that unsafe reversal without executing it.
For ||, divisor == 0 || 12 / divisor > 1 protects the division. At zero the first condition is already true. Its meaning differs: no division is needed or the quotient is large. Safety does not make it equivalent to the previous && expression.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
Do not replace logical operators with bitwise ones
Single & and | are different operators and do not provide the same short-circuit protection. They may evaluate a dangerous right side. Use && and || for these guards. Full bitwise arithmetic comes later; for now understand why deleting one symbol changes the contract.
! has high precedence: !score == 0 does not mean !(score == 0). Use explicit parentheses when negating a condition, or assign a meaningful validScore name and use !validScore.

records.title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
records.text:
Range validity and start policy
The laboratory first validates loadPercent within 0…100, then permits starting when connected and load is at most 80. Load 90 is a valid percentage but starting is forbidden. Separating valid from can_start distinguishes invalid data from a legitimate policy rejection.
Test −1, 0, 80, 81, 100, 101 and a separate disconnected case. Predict both flags. The short-circuit diagram explicitly names a skipped operand so meaning does not depend on color.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Linear search: Sequentially checking elements until a match or the end.
Binary search: Roughly halving a suitable ordered search range.
lower_bound: The first position whose element is not less than the key.
upper_bound: The first position whose element is greater than the key.
equal_range: The half-open interval of all key-equivalent elements.
Boundary invariant: A statement describing positions excluded on each side.
Partition: A range split by one predicate, sufficient for a particular search.
Absence witness: end or a nonmatching element after checking the boundary.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Find a first match and a duplicate interval while proving the required ordering is available.
Prove a binary-search invariant.
Implement lower_bound with a half-open interval.
Handle absent keys and duplicates.
Distinguish comparisons from iterator movement.
Validate ordering before searching.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
What does “find” mean?
Search can ask whether a key exists, where its first match is, how many matches exist, or which records satisfy a range. These answers are not interchangeable. For each target, the lab returns the target, its first matching index and its count; absence uses index −1 and count zero.
An index is a position in the current ordered collection, not a permanent record ID. Rearrangement can make an old position identify something else. Store a domain ID in the record and search for it again. Duplicate values may be allowed while duplicate IDs are rejected by a separate project contract.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Linear search as a baseline oracle
A linear scan checks items in sequence and needs no sorting. Stop at the first equality for a first match, or continue to count all matches. This is easy to inspect on small data and makes a useful independent oracle for a more complex search. Do not reuse the very boundary defect you intend to check inside the oracle.
Absence requires inspecting all n items; a first-position match needs one equality check. For one query on a small collection, sorting a copy may cost more than scanning. Start with a correct simple solution and estimate how many queries could repay an index before calling binary search unconditionally better.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Sorting is sufficient, but understand partitioning
For ascending lower_bound, element<target must hold on an initial segment and fail afterward. That is partitioning for the particular target. A fully sorted range supplies it for every target, so the lab requires sorting and checks is_sorted first. Arbitrary unsorted input does not give the algorithm a meaningful-result obligation.
Index construction and queries must use compatible ordering. Sorting records by name does not prepare an ID search. Silently sorting inside every query changes both cost and position meaning. Design the required index and specify when mutations require rebuilding it.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
A half-open lower-bound invariant
Maintain first=0 and last=n. Elements before first are known to be smaller than target; elements from last through n−1 are known not to be smaller. The insertion position lies between first and last, including both boundary positions. While first<last, mid=first+(last−first)/2 identifies a valid element to compare.
If a[mid]<target, the boundary is to its right, so set first=mid+1. Otherwise set last=mid because mid may itself be the first suitable position. Both branches strictly decrease last−first, proving termination. At first==last the boundary is found, but it can be n; reading a[n] remains invalid.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Duplicates, upper bound and safe absence
lower_bound returns the first element not less than target; upper_bound returns the first strictly greater element. Their half-open interval contains all ties, and vector-iterator subtraction gives the count. On [1,2,2,2,9] for target 2 the positions are 1 and 4, giving three matches. For absent target 3 both boundaries equal 4.
Check whether the matching interval is empty before reading a record. With custom comparators, lower_bound calls comp(element,target), while upper_bound calls comp(target,element); this matters when searching structures with a numeric key. Successful compilation does not prove the two predicates describe the same order.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Comparisons, advances and total cost
Each comparison roughly halves the candidates, giving logarithmic comparison growth. A vector supports constant-time midpoint access, allowing logarithmic search on a prepared range. A standard boundary search on a forward range can have logarithmic comparisons yet linear iterator advances. Do not call their total time identical from comparison counts alone.
The lab reads n values and q queries, validates input and ordering, then searches. Total processing includes O(n+q) reading and O(n) validation, not just O(q log n). A service reusing an index can account for preparation separately, but that must match the actual data lifecycle.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
How boundary logic fails
Using first=mid instead of mid+1 can leave a one-candidate interval unchanged. On paper, first=3,last=4 gives mid=3, so length does not decrease. There is no need to run an infinite loop in the working runtime: demonstrate the broken variant or simulate a bounded number of steps separately.
(first+last)/2 can overflow for large boundaries; first+(last−first)/2 avoids that problem under valid bounds. Do not mix half-open update rules with a closed interval or use size−1 on an empty array. Choose one convention and align every update, condition and final check with it.

records.title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
records.text:
Tests and the transition to recursion
Compare the library interval with an independent linear count on empty, singleton, all-equal and mixed collections. Query before the minimum, the minimum, a duplicate, a gap, the maximum and after it. Unsorted input should be explicitly rejected, not yield an arbitrary position. Missing queries and extra tokens test the application contract too.
The cumulative practicum connects stable record sorting with boundary search under the same key. Keep original labels and explain preparation separately from querying. Recursion comes next: shrinking a subproblem remains central, but function calls store continuation state instead of only two loop variables.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Branch: An alternative control path chosen by a condition.
Iteration: One execution of a loop body.
Counter: A variable recording a step.
Sum invariant: After k steps, sum includes exactly the processed even values.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
An algorithm follows a definite route: statements run in sequence, branches choose paths and loops repeat operations.
Distinguish sequencing, branching and loops.
Trace a loop's variables.
Explain continuation versus termination.
Test boundary values.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Sequencing is ordered execution
In a simple program, reading input comes before computation and printing. Reordering these steps may use an uninitialized or outdated result.
Record the values that exist after each statement to reason about execution precisely.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Conditions select an alternative
if executes its body when its condition is true; else handles the alternative. n%2==0 tests whether an integer is even.
Test both outcomes. Inclusive and exclusive comparisons behave differently at the boundary.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Loops describe repeated operations
To sum even values from 1 to n, we visit each k and add it to sum only if it is even. A loop avoids manually repeating similar statements.
for groups initialization, continuation and update. With while, updating the counter normally belongs in the loop body.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
A trace reveals state
At n=5, k visits 1 through 5. The sum changes at k=2 and k=4, reaching 6.
Write (k,sum) after each iteration. The invariant says that sum contains precisely the processed even integers.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Termination and input bounds
Without advancing k, a loop guarded by k<=n may not terminate. Huge inputs can also consume time or overflow an integer.
Our exercise limits n to 0..10000, where the sum fits a 32-bit int. Broader programs must choose appropriate bounds and types.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Zero iterations and the loop boundary
In for (int k=1; k<=n; ++k), initialization happens once, the condition is checked before each iteration, and ++k runs after the body. For n=0, the condition is false immediately and the sum stays 0. For n=6, 6 is included: 2+4+6=12. Replacing <= with < loses the last item when it is even. The parity check inside the body does not replace the loop condition.

records.title: Control flow: sequence, decisions and iteration
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
Integer inputs must fit the Code Studio int type. Failed extraction (text instead of a number or end of input) produces invalid; no further calculation is performed.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Stability: Preserving the original relative order of equivalent elements.
Insertion: Adding the next item to a sorted prefix by shifting.
Selection: Finding the minimum of the suffix and placing it at the boundary.
Bubble: Comparing neighbors and exchanging inverted pairs.
Invariant: A property true before and after each iteration.
Strict comparison: A less-than relation excluding equality.
Shift: Moving an item to an adjacent position to make room.
Adaptivity: Work that depends on order already present in the input.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Develop bubble, selection and insertion sorts while checking order, element preservation and the relative order of tied keys.
Prove a sorted-prefix invariant.
Trace insertion, selection and bubble with duplicate keys.
Check stability using original indices.
Separate comparisons, shifts and swaps.
Choose an algorithm for a small nearly ordered collection.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
The complete sorting contract
For ascending integers, the result must be ordered and contain every original value with the same multiplicity. The second condition preserves the multiset. Replacing all items with zero can pass an order check but is not sorting. Records must retain their associated fields too: a key cannot be detached from its name or ID.
The lab automatically assigns each record an original position. key determines order while original makes rearrangements observable. n=0 is valid and prints an empty line. Reject out-of-range, missing or extra data before reporting a result; a partial output would otherwise resemble a successfully sorted collection.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
A comparison predicate defines the order
For our integers, a<b means “a should precede b”. Strictness requires that an item never precede itself. Transitivity connects three values: a<b and b<c imply a<c. Tied keys mean neither precedes the other. General library sorting requires a strict weak order, rather than an arbitrary function returning bool.
a<=b is not strict: tied values make it true in both directions. Do not pass it to a standard sort as an experiment; violating a library precondition is unsafe. Check the wrong rule separately as a relation on a small table. Shifting tied elements in insertion sort is a different, safely observable experiment about stability.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Bubble: a finalized suffix
Scan left to right, swapping neighbors when the right key is smaller. After a pass, a maximum of the processed prefix is at its right end. The next pass can stop one position earlier because a suffix contains finalized maxima. The termination variant is the length of the unfinished region, which decreases after each pass.
Without early exit, neighbor comparisons total n(n−1)/2 even on sorted input. A changed flag can stop after a swap-free pass; reset it before each pass. Strict comparisons and adjacent swaps preserve tied-record order. For an empty vector, guard with end>1 instead of computing an unprotected size−1.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Selection: minima on the left
At step i, find best, the position of a minimum key in [i,n), then swap records a[i] and a[best]. The invariant says positions before i contain their final smallest elements. The inner search does not mutate the array; the outer step finalizes one position. Trace best separately before doing the swap.
This version uses quadratic minimum-search comparisons in both best and worst cases. At most n−1 nontrivial swaps are needed, though the shown code also assigns when best==i. Ordinary selection sort is unstable: swapping first and last in (2,A),(2,B),(1,C) places B before A. Fewer swaps alone do not make it best for every record type.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Insertion: a sorted prefix
Before step i, [0,i) is sorted. Copy a[i] into saved, then shift larger keys right until the insertion position is found. saved is necessary because shifting overwrites its original cell. After assigning a[j]=saved, [0,i+1) is sorted and contains the same multiset of records.
Test j>0 before reading a[j−1], protecting the left boundary. Stop shifting on equal keys so the new item stays after earlier ties; this gives stability. For sorted input with n≥1, there are n−1 key comparisons; reverse distinct input needs n(n−1)/2 shifts. Near-sortedness benefits insertion much more than selection.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Stability and multiple keys
Stability does not make every input permutation produce the same result: tied keys retain that particular input order. If you need “score, then ID”, specify both keys. For equal-time events, retaining arrival order may be a domain requirement that an extra name sort would violate.
Distinguish the library promises used in the next lesson: ordinary sort does not guarantee stability, while stable_sort does. Neither removes comparator requirements. First trace labels A and B manually, then state what your ranking needs and which test distinguishes the implementations.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Checking a sort independently
Check neighboring order, then length and value frequencies; for a stable version also check original order inside each tied-key group. Distinct-only data cannot test stability. Empty, singleton, equal, reverse, sorted and duplicate-containing inputs represent different classes, not decorative variations of one example.
For a small collection, independently write the expected result. Later we add a library oracle and property checks, but comparing two functions with the same defect is not independence. Input permutation and sorting twice provide useful extra checks. They strengthen tests without replacing invariants and boundary reasoning.

records.title: Sorting: contracts, stability and invariants
records.text:
Choosing an implementation and the task boundary
Manual sorts here teach state, invariants and cost. Normal development should first consider an appropriate library algorithm. Selection depends on size, data structure, comparison/move cost and stability requirements. Success on 32 items is not evidence for the fastest algorithm on large logs.
Submit stable insertion source, a one-pass trace, expected and actual cases, and a worst-case shift argument. As an extension, add bubble’s early exit without changing its contract. The next lesson separates a container from traversal through iterators and introduces standard algorithms as composable tools.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
LIFO: last in, first out.
FIFO: first in, first out.
Adapter: an operation interface over a suitable container.
top: access to a nonempty stack’s top.
front: access to a nonempty queue’s beginning.
Undo snapshot: a prior state preserved to reverse a successful operation.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
Choose LIFO or FIFO, check emptiness, and connect module skills in a verifiable project.
Explain: LIFO and FIFO
Trace: Operations and preconditions
Justify: Queueing and execution
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not add history for a rejected command. Do not read front/top on an empty adapter.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
LIFO and FIFO
std::stack<T> from <stack> provides last in, first out: the most recently pushed element is removed first. std::queue<T> from <queue> provides first in, first out: the earliest element is processed first. These are access disciplines, not physical representations.
Both adapt an underlying suitable container. A teaching queue does not require reimplementing a linked list. Justify the choice by ordering, size, and operations; arbitrary indexed access is not part of these interfaces.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
Operations and preconditions
push adds an element, empty checks absence, and size gives the count. stack top reads the top; queue front reads the beginning and back the end. These read operations require a nonempty adapter.
pop removes an element but returns no value. Read the required value with top/front before pop. Do not retain a reference to the removed element. Calling pop on empty is not a valid way to discover emptiness.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
Undo as state history
For a small catalogue, save the previous validated state in a stack before a successful mutation. undo restores top and removes it. A rejected command must not add history, or undo would depend on user errors.
A whole-state copy is simple but uses memory proportional to record count per step. Inverse operations are more compact but harder to justify. The project uses bounded snapshots and explicit record and command limits.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
Queueing and execution
A parser validates command syntax and queues the command. The executor reads front and applies domain checks to the current state. A syntactically valid command can still be rejected because stock is insufficient at execution time.
Order matters: add followed by remove can differ from the reverse order. Process the finite queue sequentially and print one result per command for reproducibility. Concurrency and blocking queues are outside this lesson.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
Project integration
The final project uses a record vector, a queue of typed commands, a stack of snapshots for undo, contracted functions, and text import/export. The previous lesson’s list remains a separate learning artifact with a justified comparison rather than an unnecessary catalogue dependency.
Split the work into parsing, domain operations, report formatting, and main. Build the application and test driver separately. Assessment includes design explanations and original tests; a working reference does not prove learner mastery.

records.title: Stacks, queues, and the final command catalogue
records.text:
Order tests and final defence
The lab supplies identical values to a stack and queue and compares reverse and original order. Test empty, singleton, and duplicate inputs. Guard every top/front with empty and read before each pop.
For the project, demonstrate rejection without mutation, two undos, empty history, a malformed file, and a saved-report roundtrip. In the defence explain ownership, bounds, and complexity, then change one requirement and add a test. This provides evidence of independent understanding.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
stdin: Standard input. Nexus supplies a finite character sequence followed by end of input.
Formatted extraction: Reading a typed value with >> according to parsing and stream-state rules.
fail(): Reports failed extraction or a more serious error; a value after failure is not treated as validated input.
eof(): Reports end of input already encountered rather than predicting future extraction success.
std::string: A library type for a sequence of characters; string algorithms are studied separately.
std::getline: Reads through a delimiter, usually newline; the delimiter is extracted but not included in the result.
std::ws: Consumes leading whitespace, including newlines and blank lines, up to a nonwhitespace character or end of input.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Handle valid and malformed input, inspect a remaining newline, and finish the module with an exact file-transfer calculation.
Read numbers with cin and check success before use.
Distinguish fail, eof, empty input, and a line ending.
Explain std::string, getline, and std::ws behavior.
Use fixed/setprecision without claiming exact internal double representation.
Implement a strict contract, prove integer bounds, and preserve a project test report.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Session 1. Reading is an operation with a result
std::cin >> count attempts to parse an int into an existing object. >> here extracts from a stream rather than shifting bits. Normal formatted extraction skips leading whitespace. cin >> a >> b extracts sequentially but may fail before reading the second value.
if (!(std::cin >> count)) checks failure of the operation. In this condition the stream indicates whether its post-read state is usable; ! negates that result. On failure we print invalid and return before using the number. Parsing success does not establish the domain range, which requires a separate check.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
A line ending is not end of input
Nexus supplies stdin as a finite buffer. After its last character, extraction can encounter EOF, end of input. In a live terminal, Enter normally adds a newline without closing the stream; more input may still arrive. A strict whole-tail check using ws can therefore wait for end of input in a live terminal.
eof() reports an already-set state, not whether another number exists. Do not replace extraction checks with while(!cin.eof()). Our finite-input task checks the actual extraction first and then, after ws, rejects a nonwhitespace tail.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Stream state and evidence-based rejection
fail() reports failed reading or bad state; eof() reports an encountered end. Both can be true when reading a number from an empty buffer. Successfully extracting the final number without trailing whitespace can set eof without an extraction failure. Thus eof alone does not mean an invalid number.
We stop processing on error here. Recovery with clear and discarding damaged input needs a separate policy and usually a loop; it is not a hidden requirement. An input number too large for long long must cause extraction failure rather than become trusted calculation data.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Session 2. Strings, remaining delimiters, and getline
<string> supplies std::string, a ready-made text type. std::string line; starts empty. std::getline(std::cin, line) stores characters before the newline and consumes the newline itself. After cin >> count that newline often remains, so the next getline can successfully obtain an empty line.
std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, name) first removes all leading whitespace, then reads text. It suits a name without significant leading spaces but destroys blank lines and indentation. Do not use it when an empty line is meaningful data. The comma separates arguments to a library function; no authored functions are required.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
A strict numeric contract and its tail
Integer extraction can successfully read the initial 8 in 8.5 and leave .5. Extraction success alone therefore does not prove that the entire input contains exactly the required integer fields. After all fields, use cin >> ws and check eof(): .5 or extra remains and is rejected. A whitespace-only tail is permitted.
The task uses the environment’s ordinary numeric format without changing locale. A C++ source literal 010 was octal; stdin text follows stream formatting and need not reproduce source-literal grammar. Parsing rules, not visual similarity, define the contract.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Output formatting is a separate decision
<iomanip> supplies setprecision. std::fixed selects fixed-point formatting and std::setprecision(2) then requests two fractional digits. The setting affects subsequent output on that stream. It changes text representation without making double exact decimal arithmetic.
Do not print prompts when the comparison contract requires only the answer. stdin already supplies input separately. Preserve exit status and exact newlines for manual checking; interface status text is not part of stdout.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Practicum C: input and object identity
Read stock within 0…100, reject extra input, and create a snapshot, reference, and pointer to live stock. Issue at most three and report initial stock, remainder, and issued quantity. &alias == selected checks that both paths identify the same object without printing a numeric address.
This combines the first eleven lessons with input. It creates no new progress IDs and does not automatically push code to the cloud. Preserve source and report normally; CI execution of references is not grading a learner submission.

records.title: Standard input and output: data contracts and a verifiable project
records.text:
Module project: units and exact rounding
Input m r h: m is MiB, 1024 × 1024 bytes; r is kbit/s, 1000 bits per second; h is overhead as a percentage of payload bits. Ranges are 0…1000000 MiB, 1…1000000 kbit/s, and 0…100 percent. This is a constant-rate model rather than a real-network timing promise.
num = m × 1024 × 1024 × 8 × (100+h), den = 100 × r × 1000. Round upward to seconds using num/den + (num%den != 0). The comparison produces bool, converted to 0 or 1 in the sum. Maximum num is 1677721600000000 and den at most 100000000000; long long suffices and multiplication begins with long long.
stdout contains seconds, seconds/60, and seconds%60 separated by spaces and a final newline. This ensures seconds = 60 × minutes + remainder with remainder 0…59. Invalid, incomplete, fractional, overflowing, or extra nonwhitespace input yields only invalid. Add two original cases and explain which defect they expose.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
Owner: an object managing the lifetime of stored elements.
View: access to another object’s elements under an explicit lifetime constraint.
size: the number of existing elements.
capacity: vector storage capacity before reallocation is needed.
reserve: increasing available capacity without creating elements.
Invalidation: loss of validity of an earlier address or view.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
Choose a container according to size requirements and pass its data to a function without losing bounds.
Explain: Why three types exist
Trace: Size is not capacity
Justify: span passes a range
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not use a span after vector reallocation; create it after filling the vector.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
Why three types exist
std::array<int,3> is an object containing three ints with its size encoded in the type. std::vector<int> owns a sequence whose size can change. std::span<const int> is a non-owning view of existing ints and their count.
Angle brackets supply arguments to a library template: the element type and, for array, the extent. You do not need to author a template yet. Include <array>, <vector>, and <span> for their corresponding names.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
Size is not capacity
vector.size() counts existing elements; capacity() counts how many can fit without reallocation. reserve(10) provides capacity but leaves size at zero. After reserve, v[0] is invalid until push_back or resize has created that element.
push_back(value) appends an element; empty() tests size()==0. Teaching programs bound the sequence to at most 100 values. In an exception-disabled environment, allocation failure is not promised to be catchable; do not use it as normal input validation.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
Traversal and auto
for(int value : values) obtains a copy of each element. for(const auto& value : values) reads without copying; auto deduces a static type and is not dynamic typing. Mutating elements requires a non-const auto& reference.
Use an index when position matters. Compare it with size() and avoid subtracting one from a zero unsigned size. Prove !empty() before accessing the last element; front and back also require a nonempty container.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
span passes a range
sum(std::span<const int> values) accepts a read-only range. Compatible arrays, vectors, and built-in arrays can supply it. Inside, size(), empty(), [], and range-for are available; the function does not own the elements’ memory.
An empty span is valid when the algorithm handles it. In C++20 these types’ operator[] is not input validation: the index must be below size(). Do not execute out-of-bounds accesses as demonstrations; identify the violated precondition on paper.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
View lifetime
The owner must remain alive throughout span use. When a growing vector reallocates, pointers, references, and spans into the old buffer become invalid. reserve may reduce reallocations but cannot replace a lifetime argument.
Finish modifying a container before creating a short-lived span, then process it without resizing the owner. Do not retain a view into a local vector after its function returns. const in span<const int> restricts writes through the view but does not extend lifetime.

records.title: array, vector, and span: ownership and views
records.text:
Choice and evidence
Use array for a small fixed set, vector for a dynamic count, and span for a viewing parameter. This separates storage from the algorithm. Linear summation needs O(n) time and O(1) additional memory regardless of the owner.
Test the same function with three owners and an empty view. Separately record size before and after reserve and push_back. Next, compare these abstractions with a traditional array while preserving identical boundary rules.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
failbit: failure of formatted extraction or a similar operation.
Record boundary: the point where one logical record ends.
eofbit: a flag indicating an already encountered end.
badbit: a flag indicating a serious stream error.
clear: changing state flags without removing buffered input.
istringstream: an input stream over a separate string.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
Distinguish eof, fail, and bad, preserve record boundaries, and recover under an explicit policy.
Explain: Flags describe a past operation
Trace: Reset state and remove the cause
Justify: Remainders after operator>>
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not treat fail&&eof as a successful number. Do not discard blank records using ws.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
Flags describe a past operation
good() means no error-state flags are set. eof() reports an encountered end, fail() tests failbit or badbit, and bad() reports a serious stream error. bool(stream) checks for absence of failbit and badbit; eofbit alone need not make it false.
Successfully extracting a final number without trailing whitespace can produce eof=true and fail=false. An oversized final numeric token may set both. eof alone therefore cannot distinguish success, empty exhaustion, and malformed input.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
Reset state and remove the cause
clear() resets flags but does not remove an invalid buffered character. ignore(max,'\n') can discard a damaged line; obtain max from numeric_limits<streamsize>::max(). Clear first and then consume input, otherwise ignore may not proceed.
Recovery is a format decision, not a universal patch. If each line is one record, skipping to the newline preserves the next record boundary. With multiline records, that strategy may destroy useful data and needs a different protocol.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
A line as the parsing unit
getline obtains a line, then istringstream from <sstream> parses only that line. A local parser failure does not poison the main cin state. Count accepted and rejected records and continue with the next line.
After required fields, consume permitted whitespace and check the local line’s end. Under a strict contract, 12x is not the integer 12: numeric extraction may stop before x. Give empty lines an explicit policy; the lab rejects them.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
Remainders after operator>>
After cin>>n, a newline commonly remains. The next getline receives the current line’s remainder, possibly empty. Preserve that remainder when significant. If the next record starts on another line, explicitly finish the current record under the format.
std::ws consumes all leading whitespace, including blank lines, not just one newline. Do not apply it before getline when blank lines or leading spaces matter. Decide which characters may be discarded before choosing an operation.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
Bounding the work
Even valid streams need row-count and line-size limits. The lab permits at most 100 lines of at most 200 bytes, with one number from -1000 to 1000 per line. Resource-limit violations produce overall invalid; a malformed individual record increments rejected.
This distinction separates data errors from environmental failures. Nexus buffers finite stdin before running; a large network stream would need a streaming limit before accumulating a whole line. That larger scale is not claimed here.

records.title: Stream states and reliable line parsing
records.text:
Recovery evidence
Use valid, bad, valid and establish that the final record is processed. Add an empty line, a number without a final newline, an oversized numeric token, and an extra field. Check accepted count, rejection count, and sum separately.
Preserve each line boundary and the local parser flags. Next, turn these cases into repeatable unit and integration tests; a Run button by itself does not establish quality.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
Field: a named component of a structure object.
Record invariant: a condition true of every valid state.
Aggregate: a simple composite object supporting memberwise initialization.
Record copy: a separate object initialized from field values.
Failure atomicity: a rejected operation preserves the previous state.
Padding: layout bytes that are not data fields.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
Group related fields and mutate a record only after validating the whole operation.
Explain: Declaring a record
Trace: A record copy and a reference
Justify: Validate, then commit
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Rejection must preserve the whole record, not merely stock. Do not serialize sizeof(struct) bytes as a portable format.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
Declaring a record
struct Item { int id{}; int stock{}; }; defines a type with two fields that are public by default. The closing brace needs a semicolon. Item item{7,12} creates an object; item.stock accesses that object’s field.
{} initializers establish defined initial values. Fields may have different types, such as string name and int stock. A structure is neither a database table nor automatic validation: domain rules determine valid values.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
A record copy and a reference
Item backup=item copies field values. Changing backup.stock does not change item.stock. const Item& reads the original without a copy; Item& permits mutation. Choose according to intent and document which fields may change.
Inserting a copy into vector<Item> stores a separate record. A reference to an element can be invalidated by vector reallocation, just like a span. Do not retain it across push_back without establishing address stability.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
A domain invariant
For stock, require id>0 and 0<=stock<=1000. issue(amount) is allowed only when 0<=amount<=stock. Success reduces stock and leaves id unchanged; rejection leaves the whole record unchanged.
A public struct does not prevent assigning negative stock. At this stage, functions and tests enforce discipline. Module 5 will use encapsulation to restrict access; do not claim the structure already protects its own data.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
Validate, then commit
Check the existing record and argument first. Compute a temporary new value, establish its bounds, and then assign. A single mutation point makes the absence of partial updates easier to establish.
