When several fields change, prepare a candidate copy and replace the original only after every check passes. This is an in-memory transaction pattern, not a promise of filesystem or Cloud Sync transactions.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
A collection of records
A vector<Item> stores catalogue records in one logical collection. Searching by id is O(n); uniqueness requires checking before insertion. An id field neither creates an index nor automatically guarantees uniqueness.
Print named fields rather than relying on raw memory layout. sizeof(Item) may include padding. Dumping an arbitrary structure’s bytes is not a portable storage format; a textual format follows in the files lesson.

records.title: Structures: records, invariants, and updates
records.text:
Before-and-after tests
Test issuing zero, issuing all stock, excessive and negative requests, and an invalid original record. Compare every field before and after rejection. Separately verify independence of the original and its backup copy.
Evidence consists of source, state tables, and an invariant explanation. Next, an enumeration distinguishes status from arbitrary integers, while variant represents commands of different shapes without reading inactive storage.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Function template: A family of functions parameterized by types or values.
Class template: A definition of a family of concrete types through parameters.
Instantiation: Forming a required specialization from a template definition.
Deduction: Inferring template arguments from call conditions.
Concept: A named compile-time constraint on template arguments.
Std integral: A standard constraint recognizing integer types.
Span: A nonowning view of a contiguous sequence.
Value contract: Data restrictions not proven by a concept alone.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Generalize an operation for two types and separate type requirements from value bounds.
Deduce T for both smaller calls.
Analyze conflicting int and long arguments.
Check sum on an empty span.
Compile the separate double rejection.
Justify laboratory arithmetic bounds.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Generalizing from two cases
If one operation is needed for int and long, duplication hides common structure and risks inconsistent fixes. A function template describes a family of functions parameterized by type. template<class T> introduces T for use in parameters and the body. This does not erase types: the compiler forms concrete specializations.
Solve the task for one type first and list its required operations. smaller compares two values and returns one by value. It needs comparison and result copying, not inheritance from a common base. The integral concept intentionally narrows this example to integer types, giving the teaching contract a clear domain.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Deducing a type argument
For smaller(3,7), both arguments deduce T as int. For smaller(9L,4L), they deduce long. In smaller(3,7L), the deductions conflict; the compiler need not invent an arbitrary common type. Align types explicitly or provide a template argument while understanding the conversion. Do not conceal data loss with a forced cast.
Template parameters and ordinary function parameters act at different stages. T is chosen during compilation, while numeric values can arrive at runtime. Different values of n alone do not require a template. An ordinary function suffices when types and operations are unchanged. Generalization should remove meaningful duplication rather than merely add syntax.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
A class template
Buffer<T> defines a family of classes, each storing vector<T>. Buffer<int> and Buffer<long long> are different concrete types. The vector is an established owner, so we do not reimplement memory management. append and sum provide a small interface around the chosen operation.
Instantiation checks constraints and the required code. An error can appear at a specialization's use rather than near the original definition. Read the diagnostic from the call towards the first violated requirement. Do not edit an arbitrary library file to fix an unfamiliar specialization error; identify the type supplied by your code first.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Concepts express requirements
In C++20 a concept is a named constraint on a template argument. std::integral from concepts recognizes integer types. template<std::integral T> constrains selection before the body is checked. The negative example rejects smaller(1.0,2.0) because of that constraint, although comparing doubles is otherwise meaningful.
A concept checks expressible compile-time requirements rather than proving every mathematical property. integral does not prevent sum overflow or promise that input values will be small. Value ranges, complexity and side effects remain documented and tested contracts. Successful compilation does not establish correctness for every value of a type.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
A range without ownership
The laboratory sum accepts std::span<const T>, a sized sequence without ownership transfer or permission to modify elements. The call explicitly constructs a span from a vector and specifies T. This separates element type from its owner. The owner must outlive the call because a span does not extend lifetime.
Deducing T from a span parameter need not first convert a vector into a span. The example therefore writes sum<int>(std::span<const int>{a}), exposing both boundaries. A range-based interface is a possible later generalization, but would distract from template fundamentals here. First explain the owner and why reading the view is valid.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
The arithmetic contract boundary
The laboratory limits size to twenty and each element to plus or minus one hundred. The absolute sum therefore cannot exceed two thousand and fits both int and long long. This argument uses value bounds and element count. The same template without those limits could overflow a signed type; integral alone does not prevent it.
For production summation choose a policy: wider accumulation, checked arithmetic or a documented precondition. Do not widen types without analysis, because even long long has limits. Separate the reusable algorithm from its concrete input contract, then check empty input, negative values and the largest permitted sum. These cases connect templates to earlier testing lessons.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Definitions and builds
A template definition generally needs to be available at the point of instantiation, so small definitions belong in a guarded header. An ordinary function defined in a header without suitable rules can violate the ODR, while templates have their own conditions for multiple definitions. Do not apply an everything-in-cpp rule indiscriminately.
The final project defines bounded in domain.hpp and ordinary Board methods in domain.cpp. Several translation units include the header; its guard prevents repeated inclusion within one unit. That does not replace linking rules. Do not include domain.cpp: translationUnits names separately compiled sources that are linked together.

records.title: Templates and constrained generalization
records.text:
Evidence of the learning outcome
The laboratory invokes one operation for int and long long and compares results on the same sequence. A separate negative double example must fail to compile. Save successful sources, inputs, results and a constraint explanation. Keep the intentionally invalid call out of the file that must execute successfully.
Compare the template with duplicated functions and a virtual interface. For summing homogeneous values, a template expresses compile-time structure; a user-selected runtime strategy needs a different mechanism. The next lesson combines these tools in a maintainable application and checks that architectural changes preserve observable behaviour.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
Regression: recurrence of a previously fixed defect.
Oracle: an independent rule determining the expected result.
Unit test: checking one operation through its interface.
Integration test: checking several parts working together.
Mutation: a safe implementation change used to assess test discrimination.
Exit code: the numeric status returned by a program.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
Build a small test driver and distinguish a program defect from a build error or environment limitation.
Explain: An expectation before execution
Trace: Unit and integration
Justify: Diagnosis by phase
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not derive expected values by running the function under test. Do not classify provider limits as learner knowledge errors.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
An expectation before execution
A test has initial data, an action, and an independently derived expectation. Copying the current output as the expectation merely preserves a possible defect. For a small sum, derive and explain the result manually.
First list input classes: empty range, one element, several elements, boundaries, and rejection. checkedArea needs valid-dimension tests and output-preservation tests on failure. These are different properties requiring distinct checks.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
Unit and integration
A unit test calls a small function directly. An integration test runs main with textual input and checks parsing, computation, and output together. Passing the first does not imply the second because text conversion can be wrong.
A driver counts failures, prints a clear summary, and returns zero on success or nonzero on failure. Check stderr separately. A PASS message is insufficient if the exit code indicates failure.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
assert and external validation
assert from <cassert> supports internal development-time expectations. It may disappear with NDEBUG, so input reading, range validation, and required side effects must not occur only inside assert.
The lab harness uses explicit if checks and a failure counter so results do not depend on NDEBUG. assert may additionally check an already computed internal property, but cannot replace a clear invalid response to external input.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
Diagnosis by phase
A syntax error or unknown name is a compilation failure. A missing function definition commonly fails at linking. Wrong stdout from a built program is a logic defect. Unsupported exceptions or environment quotas are separate provider limitations.
An intentional compile-negative is a control expected to fail to build. Do not present it as a working lab solution. Compiler messages vary; check the phase and meaning rather than the entire message byte for byte.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
The defect-fixing cycle
Reproduce a defect with minimal input first. Record the expectation and cause. Add a test that fails on the wrong implementation, fix the implementation, and rerun the complete set including previously passing cases.
A mutation experiment changes one safe operation, such as > to >= when counting positives. If every test stays green, the set cannot distinguish the implementations. Add a zero-valued case; do not infer that no defect exists.

records.title: Testing: contracts, defects, and regression
records.text:
Limits of the evidence
Tests cover a finite case set and do not replace bounds or lifetime arguments. UBSan detects some violations, but silence does not prove complete safety. Combine tests with invariants.
Preserve versioned source, build instructions, inputs, expectations, actual results, and verification limits. Lesson rubrics remain manual; automatic Mastery is not claimed. Next, separate the application and driver into compilation units.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
Token: A meaningful lexical unit such as a name, literal, or operator; not necessarily one character or a word separated by spaces.
Identifier: A name form used in declarations and references to program entities.
Keyword: A word with a special grammatical role, such as int or return; it cannot be declared as an ordinary quantity name.
Literal: A value written directly in source, such as 250 or "duration_ms=".
Naming convention: A team agreement about readable names that may be stricter than the language syntax.
Renaming: A consistent name change in a declaration and all corresponding uses while preserving meaning.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
Read source as a sequence of meaningful parts, choose safe names, and rename them without changing behavior.
Distinguish keywords, identifiers, literals, operators, and punctuation.
Explain case, whitespace, quotes, and token boundaries.
Choose meaningful names with units and avoid reserved forms.
Rename quantities and demonstrate unchanged stdout for several data variants.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
Source is not simply words between spaces
Consider int count = 4;. Here int is a keyword, count is an identifier, = is an operator in the initializer syntax, 4 is an integer literal, and ; is a delimiter. Whitespace helps separate pieces but is usually not a language token itself. In count*4, the tokens remain distinct without spaces.
In std::cout << "duration_ms=" << count;, :: spans two characters but is one token; so does <<. A string literal may contain spaces: "total length" is not split into two identifiers. Header inclusion has special preprocessing rules; do not count the pieces of #include with a homemade whitespace splitter.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
Token boundaries affect meaning
int count=4; and int count = 4; declare the same object. But intcount = 4; no longer contains the int keyword: it contains a different name. Similarly, totalCount is one identifier while total Count is two. Inserting whitespace at an arbitrary position is not always formatting.
Indentation and line breaks outside literals help readability. Inside quotes, a space becomes output data: "length cm=" and "length_cm=" produce different strings. Therefore, formatting changes require a behavior comparison rather than visual inspection alone. Do not combine reformatting with a formula repair in one experiment.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
The names we choose in this course
Our examples use ASCII Latin letters, digits, and, when useful, underscores; a digit cannot come first. ASCII is a basic character set containing Latin letters and digits. sampleCount, count2, and period_ms follow our convention. A hyphen or space is not part of such a name: sample-count is parsed as names and subtraction.
This is a course convention, not a claim that C++20 forbids all non-Latin identifiers: specified additional characters are permitted. We restrict the alphabet for convenient typing and portability. Case matters: totalMs and totalMS are distinct names. Choose one style, such as lowerCamelCase, and use it consistently.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
Keywords and reserved forms
int, return, const, and while have special language roles. You encountered while in Module 1; you do not need to write a loop here. A quantity cannot be named return. cout is not a keyword: it is a library name inside std. Editor coloring is a hint and does not replace compiler checks.
Some identifier-shaped forms are reserved for the implementation. Avoid double underscores anywhere and an underscore followed by an uppercase letter; our convention avoids any leading underscore. A compiler accepting a reserved name does not make its use valid: some reservation violations require no diagnostic. Thus a successful build is insufficient evidence of a good name.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
A name conveys role and unit
a*b hides the meaning of a duration calculation. sampleCount * periodMs states that a sample count is multiplied by a period in milliseconds to obtain durationMs. The Ms suffix documents the unit. int does not distinguish milliseconds from centimeters; a unit error can compile successfully.
Do not encode an incidental current value in a name: samples4 becomes misleading when 4 changes to 6. Avoid restating the entire formula in an excessively long name. A useful name answers what the quantity means in the task. Internal durationMs and the external label duration_ms= may follow different conventions; renaming an object need not change the output contract.

records.title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
records.text:
Safe renaming is a small, verifiable change
Record the original stdout first. Rename one declaration and all its uses, then build and compare output. Continue with the next name afterward. Text search helps, but blindly replacing a everywhere can corrupt main and labels. Match word boundaries and review every replacement.
Compare the baseline and at least two other initial-value sets. With an unchanged formula, before and after output should agree for each set. This checks behavior on selected cases, not every possible program. The diagram below manually classifies one selected statement; it is not a lexer for arbitrary C++.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Decomposition: Breaking a large problem into smaller problems with explicit boundaries.
Function: A named operation that receives arguments and can return a result.
Function contract: The expected inputs, outputs and valid calling conditions.
Cohesion: How closely a component's responsibilities belong together.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Complex software becomes easier to build and verify when decomposed into small operations with clear responsibilities.
Decompose a requirement into cohesive functions.
Specify function inputs, outputs and constraints.
Separate input validation, computation and presentation.
Use unit-level and integration-level test cases.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Start with the result the user needs
An order calculator can be described as: read input → validate → calculate → report. Instead of writing one long main, state the responsibility of each stage.
At a lower level, calculation splits into a subtotal and a discount operation. Validation enforces nonnegative values and a percentage between 0 and 100.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Define contracts before implementation details
subtotal(price,qty) computes a total under an explicit valid-input assumption. valid returns true or false for the specified bounds.
Choose names that express purpose: subtotal is more helpful than doStuff. A reporting function need not know the internals of the calculation.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Separate calculation from interaction
std::cin and std::cout belong at the application boundary. Computation functions should ideally not be tied to console interaction so the same logic can serve a UI or test.
valid and subtotal can then be examined independently. This reduces diagnostic complexity without replacing end-to-end tests.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Manage dependencies
Higher-level orchestration calls lower-level functions. When each component receives only necessary arguments, changes are more localized and tests become focused.
In the example, main handles user input but subtotal does not. This separation is a reusable architecture principle.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Diagnose a multi-step calculation
If a total is wrong, check input validation, intermediate subtotal and discount calculation in sequence. Each boundary has observable values.
For teaching we use int; professional monetary systems need explicit units, overflow policies and rounding conventions. Those are later topics in the curriculum.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Reading a function call
bool valid(...) declares a check returning true or false. Parameters receive argument values on a call; return supplies a result to the caller. In discountPrice(subtotal(price, qty), discount), the subtotal is needed first: 100 and 3 give 300, then a 10 percent discount gives 300 − 30 = 270. This data dependency does not require compressing all work into one line. Store the subtotal in a named variable while debugging.

records.title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
records.text:
Input policy and execution limits
Price and quantity are integers 0..1000; discount is 0..100. Round the saving down to whole units: total = subtotal − (subtotal·discount)/100. The bounds keep intermediate products within a 32-bit int.
Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Shape: row and column counts together with their consistency.
Row-major: elements of each row are contiguous.
Matrix row: elements with a fixed first coordinate.
Matrix column: elements with a fixed second coordinate.
Transposition: exchanging coordinate roles and dimensions.
Rectangularity: equal element counts in all rows.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Map two coordinates to an index and validate rectangular shape before computing.
Explain: Two coordinates
Trace: Nested traversal
Justify: Rectangularity and nested vectors
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: Do not test matrix code only with a square shape. Do not obtain cols from a[0] when there are no rows.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Two coordinates
A matrix has rows rows and cols columns. Element (r,c) is valid when 0<=r<rows and 0<=c<cols. In std::array<std::array<int,3>,2>, the outer size is two rows and the inner size is three columns. A built-in int a[2][3] is also an array of rows.
a[r][c] first selects a row and then its element. Swapping indices does not safely transpose an arbitrary matrix: rectangular dimensions may produce out-of-bounds access. Check both coordinates independently.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Nested traversal
The outer loop visits rows; the inner loop visits columns in the current row. Set rowSum=0 before the inner loop and initialize total once before both loops. Mixing these state levels leaves only the final row’s sum.
With rows*cols elements, a complete traversal is O(rows*cols). If either dimension is zero, there are no elements. The lab explicitly permits zero dimensions so the algorithm never depends on a[0] existing.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
A flat buffer
In row-major storage, the index is r*cols+c. The preceding r rows occupy r*cols positions, then c selects a column. In a 2x3 matrix, (1,2) maps to 5, the last of six elements. This follows from the representation rather than a magic conversion.
vector<int> data(rows*cols) creates elements, unlike reserve. Validate dimensions before multiplying. Dimensions up to 10 give at most 100 elements; values in -1000…1000 have an absolute total at most 100000.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Rectangularity and nested vectors
vector<vector<int>> can contain rows of different lengths. Its type does not establish rectangularity. Before running a matrix algorithm, verify that every row has cols elements; define cols separately when the outer vector is empty.
Flat storage simplifies the total size but requires an indexing formula. Nested storage exposes rows clearly but gives each row a separate owned buffer. Choose a representation for the required operations rather than bracket appearance.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Rows, columns, and transposition
A column sum fixes c and varies r. A square matrix’s main diagonal has r==c; a rectangular generalization has length min(rows,cols) if the contract defines it that way. Never assume square shape without validation.
A transpose has cols rows and rows columns. Write result[c*rows+r]=data[r*cols+c] into a new buffer. An in-place transpose requires another algorithm and is not an implicit requirement here.

records.title: Matrices: shape, traversal, and linear storage
records.text:
Shape tests
A square example can hide reversed dimensions. Include 2x3 and 3x2, one row, one column, and a zero dimension. Label original positions with distinct values to expose permutations.
Keep a table of (r,c,index,value), expected sums, and operation counts. Incomplete or excess input must reject the whole record as invalid. Next, character sequences introduce another distinction: a byte, a character, and a terminator are different things.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Implicit conversion: Conversion to a required type without an explicit cast in source.
Integral promotion: Promotion of a small integer type to int or unsigned int according to representability.
static_cast<T>(value): An explicit permitted conversion to T, not a universal safety check.
Narrowing: A conversion risking range or precision loss; list initialization rejects specified cases.
Unsigned modulo: Unsigned-value behavior modulo two raised to the type’s width.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Identify an operation’s type before it runs and use static_cast only with a justified intention.
Distinguish implicit conversion, promotion, and explicit static_cast.
Obtain fractional division by converting an operand before /.
Explain the selected mixed-sign example and unsigned modulo.
Check valid ranges before a potentially lossy conversion.
Use narrowing diagnostics as useful evidence.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Session 1. The common type is chosen before the operation
With two ints, total / count performs integer division. Storing the result in double afterward cannot restore the fraction. static_cast<double>(total / count) first obtains integer 3 and then double 3.0; static_cast<double>(total) / count converts an operand first and gives 3.5 for 7 and 2.
In static_cast<double>(total), static_cast selects an explicit conversion, <double> specifies the destination type, and parentheses contain the expression. It is a language operator rather than a function we authored. Use it to state justified intent; unnecessary casts can obscure meaning.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Promotions and usual arithmetic conversions
Before many integer operations, bool, char, and short undergo integral promotions: to int when it represents all source values, otherwise to unsigned int. Thus adding two chars does not necessarily yield char. Type rules, not the length of the printed number, determine the result.
After promotions, arithmetic operators choose a common type. In our double-and-int examples the integer operand converts to double. Same-sign integer types convert toward the greater rank; mixed signs need additional rules. Rank is a language ordering rather than merely sizeof. Do not replace the rules with “the larger size always wins.”

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Why −1 < 1u can be false
In this example debt is int and credit is unsigned int. Their ranks correspond, so int converts to unsigned int before comparison. −1 becomes the maximum unsigned int value and comparison with 1 is false. This follows defined conversion rules rather than a compiler defect.
Unsigned integer conversion is congruent modulo 2^N, where N is the destination width. We do not assume N=32 universally. The example compares with numeric_limits<unsigned int>::max() instead of demanding one numeric maximum. Repairing a domain comparison requires valid signs and ranges rather than blindly casting both sides to unsigned.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Session 2. static_cast is not a validator
Converting double 3.75 to int gives 3, and −3.75 gives −3: the fraction is discarded toward zero rather than rounded to the nearest integer. We execute only values whose truncated result is representable. Out-of-range floating-to-integer conversion is not a safe experiment.
Before narrowing, establish the destination range and domain rules. If a value must be a whole count, losing a fraction can be wrong even within range. static_cast does not automatically reject that domain error. int count{2.5}; usefully detects specified narrowing during the build; do not add a cast merely to silence it.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Change the type before information is lost
Widening before multiplication and converting before division solve the same design problem: choosing operation semantics before execution. Casting an already-overflowed or truncated result cannot repair the past.
Keep exact totals in integer minor units and calculate an approximate average separately. This distinguishes exact stored quantities from derived approximations. If every cent matters, formatting and rounding must be explicit contract rules rather than accidental cast consequences.

records.title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
records.text:
Verification and practicum B
For the average, test 7/2, 0/2, 10/4, and rejection of zero count. The first and third expose premature integer division; zero alone cannot. Write expected values 3.5, 0, and 2.5 before running.
Practicum B combines named stages, integer-product bounds, and a floating-point average. Reference values allow simple output; full formatting is introduced in lesson 12. The diagram compares two specific division paths rather than executing arbitrary C++ conversions.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
Alias: another name for an existing type.
Active alternative: the type of value currently held by a variant.
enum class: a distinct type with scoped enumerator names.
union: a type whose members share storage.
variant: a library type with one active alternative.
get_if: checked alternative access returning a pointer or nullptr.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
Model restricted choices and different command shapes while checking the active alternative.
Explain: enum class scopes names
Trace: using and typedef name existing types
Justify: variant stores an alternative and its tag
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: using does not create a strong type. Do not inspect bits by reading an inactive union member.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
enum class scopes names
enum class Mode { add, remove }; creates a distinct type. Values are written Mode::add and Mode::remove and do not implicitly become int. This prevents accidental mixing with another enumeration but does not validate an external numeric code.
Parse input with if or switch and explicitly map accepted tokens to enumeration values. static_cast<Mode>(number) does not establish membership in the domain set. In switch, list valid alternatives and define how unexpected states are handled.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
using and typedef name existing types
using Count=int; and typedef int Count; create aliases for int. They improve readability, but Count and int remain interchangeable. An alias does not automatically prevent a negative count or mixing units.
Prefer using for simple new declarations because name=type reads clearly. A truly distinct domain type can use a struct with checked operations; Module 5 develops that approach further.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
Why union requires discipline
Union members share storage. Writing one member does not make every other representation a valid value. Active-member and lifetime rules are more demanding than a shared address.
In a valid introductory example, assign and read the same active int member. Do not type-pun through an inactive double or label its possible output portable. Special language exceptions are unnecessary for this task.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
variant stores an alternative and its tag
std::variant<Add,Remove> from <variant> stores one active alternative and identifies it. Define command structs first, then choose an alternative while parsing a token. Using a library template does not require authoring a template.
std::get_if<Add>(&command) returns a pointer to Add or nullptr. Check it before ->amount. A wrong-type std::get involves an exception, so it is not used here: the current Clang/WASI environment disables exception support.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
Dispatch and invariants
Parsing and executing a command are different functions. The parser accepts only add and remove and checks amount. The executor examines the active alternative and then validates the stock update. Invalid input must not leave a half-prepared command.
A variant does not guarantee the domain validity of amount. With stock capped at 1000, check amount<=1000-stock before adding and amount<=stock before removing. These checks avoid calculating a known-invalid new state.

records.title: Enumerations, aliases, and variant data
records.text:
Checking the choice
Test both alternatives, an unknown command, zero amount, exceeding the stock cap, and insufficient stock. A get_if for the other type must return nullptr, which the program must not dereference.
Compare alias, enum class, union, and variant in a table covering distinct types, named values, active alternatives, and checked access. Next, move from choosing a representation to ownership: who releases a resource and who merely observes it.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
Value semantics: An independent copied value under the type's observable contract.
Copy constructor: Construction of a new object from an existing value.
Copy assignment: Replacing an existing object's value with a copy.
Move operation: An operation that can transfer resources from an eligible source.
Std move: A cast changing an expression category, not itself a resource transfer.
Moved-from state: A source's post-move state governed by its specific type contract.
Noexcept: A promise that no exception escapes a marked function.
Rule of five: Deliberate coordination of five special operations for a resource-managing type.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
Check independent copies and ownership transfer without assuming a moved-from string is empty.
Distinguish b=a at construction and later.
Predict Note after reassignment.
Justify independence of Batch b.
Check vector self-assignment.
Analyze std::move on a const string.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
A value and its independent copy
Value semantics means a copy represents an independent value. Note stores a string that manages its content. After Note b=a, changing b.text must not change a.text. Copying a pointer is different: two objects can then observe one memory region. A type's contract should explain which behaviour it provides.
Batch uses vector<int> and follows the rule of zero: compiler-generated special operations compose the member operations. A vector copy has its own elements, so changing b.values leaves the original batch intact. Check independence through observable behaviour. Equality of addresses or internal buffer layouts is not a required part of a value contract.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
Construction and assignment
T b=a creates a new object using a copy constructor, commonly taking const T&. Writing b=a after b already exists calls copy assignment. They have different starting conditions: assignment must replace an existing value correctly. Self-assignment must satisfy the contract the type claims to provide.
Ordinary domain types containing vector and string should usually retain generated operations. A type manually managing a raw resource may copy its address and cause double release. That is a reason to introduce an RAII member, rather than immediately writing four more complicated functions. A manual implementation needs a concrete requirement.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
What std::move does
std::move casts an expression to a category that permits selection of a move operation. It does not transfer or clear anything by itself. Note c=std::move(a) subsequently invokes an appropriate constructor, which may move the string. Without a suitable move operation, copying may be selected or compilation may fail.
T&& in a move constructor parameter declares an rvalue reference. A named variable is still an lvalue expression even if its type is an rvalue reference, so forwarding a member to a move operation often requires std::move. This is not a reason to add move everywhere: a const source may be copied, and moving a returned local can inhibit an optimization.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
The moved-from state
After a permitted move, standard-library types generally remain valid but with an unspecified specific state unless a tighter contract is provided. Do not assert that a moved-from string is necessarily empty. Destruction and assignment remain useful permitted operations. The example assigns reused to a.text before reading it, making the output portable.
unique_ptr has a more specific promise: transferring ownership leaves the source pointer empty. The separate example checks bool(a), while b owns the integer seven. Do not generalize this guarantee to arbitrary containers. State which type contract justifies every test involving a moved-from object.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
Noexcept and container choices
noexcept promises that an exception will not leave a function. It does not instruct the program to ignore errors: violating the promise invokes terminate. Containers can account for nonthrowing moves when preserving guarantees during reallocation. A custom special member's exception specification must match the operations performed on its members.
Do not mark arbitrary code noexcept as a speed trick. Copying a vector can allocate memory; inventing a strong guarantee does not make that allocation nonthrowing. The rule of zero lets suitable library members contribute their properties to the composed type. Actual exception guarantees are studied two lessons later, so throwing move experiments are unnecessary here.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
The rule of five signals complexity
When manual resource management requires a destructor, consider the copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment deliberately. Some can be =delete and others =default. This is the rule of five, not a requirement to permit all five operations for every type.
A sole-resource owner can be neither movable nor copyable when the surrounding system requires that restriction. Such constraints are usually unnecessary for this domain model. Choosing vector or unique_ptr delegates ownership to an established component. During review first ask whether the rule of zero is possible, and only then discuss manual special-member code.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
Laboratory: batches of values
The laboratory reads up to twenty integers between minus one hundred and one hundred into Batch a. Copy b increments each of its own elements. Then c receives a's contents through moving, and a is explicitly assigned a new vector containing forty-two. For 1 2 3 the output is 6 9 42.
The test never examines a between the move and reassignment and does not depend on optional copy elision. With an empty batch the copies remain independent, both sums are zero and reusing a is valid. Add self-assignment b=b and explain why the chosen members handle it without manual raw-memory management.

records.title: Value semantics, copying and moving
records.text:
Measuring without false conclusions
An instrumented type can count calls to explicitly selected copy and move operations. Counts in return expressions, however, depend on mandatory and permitted copy-elision rules. Do not present one observed count as a universal property of a C++ program. Fix the expression and compiler, and distinguish observable semantics from timing.
The outcome is the ability to explain copy independence, ownership transfer and safe source reuse. The project will use a Board copy as an independent state snapshot in a test. Next we separate value semantics from polymorphic interfaces, where copying a base portion can discard a derived object's behaviour.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
Variable: In these examples a named typed object with state; mutation is allowed unless the object is const.
Assignment: Replacing the value of an existing object, as in stock = 7;.
Name scope: The program region in which a name can be found under language rules.
Object lifetime: The period in which an object exists during execution, rather than a source line or merely name visibility.
Shadowing: An inner declaration with the same name hides the outer declaration during lookup in that block.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
Trace when an object is created, which name denotes it, and why a copy does not change with the original.
Distinguish initialization from later assignment.
Predict the state of an original object and an independent copy.
Determine name visibility in nested blocks and recognize shadowing.
Explain name scope versus object lifetime.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
Session 1. An object acquires state
int stock{10}; creates an object initialized to 10. stock = 7; changes that existing object rather than creating another stock. In assignment, the left side identifies the destination and the right side produces the new value. In int snapshot = stock;, a similar sign introduces the initial value of a new object.
Read statements top to bottom and record state after each. stock = stock - 3; reads the old stock, computes the difference, and stores it back. It is not the mathematical equation stock = stock − 3. These small values are safe, but range reasoning still applies.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
A copy is a snapshot, not a link
int snapshot = stock; creates a second int holding the current value of the first. Changing stock later leaves snapshot unchanged. Equal values do not imply one object. We may label them S and C in a trace; these are symbolic identifiers rather than actual memory addresses.
Print both values after changing the original to test copying. Printing stock twice does not observe snapshot at all. References and pointers are introduced in lesson eleven; do not use them as an unexplained shortcut here.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
Session 2. A block limits name scope
A standalone pair of braces can form a nested block inside main. Its statements execute in sequence. A name adjustment declared within is available after its declaration inside the block, but not after its closing brace. An outer count remains visible inside unless another count declaration hides it.
Distinguish block braces from the initializer in int count{10};. One groups statements and the other provides an initial value. Indentation highlights boundaries, but braces rather than whitespace define them.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
Shadowing creates a different object
The inner int count{3}; creates another object. count = 4; affects that object rather than the outer count{10}. After leaving the block, lookup finds the outer name again with value 10. The outer object was neither destroyed nor restored from a backup.
Shadowing is allowed in the shown nested block but often makes debugging harder. Prefer distinct meaningful names such as totalCount and batchCount in normal work. The intentional example teaches recognition of the false claim that changing the inner count changed the outer one.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
Name visibility and object existence
Scope concerns source regions and name lookup; lifetime concerns execution. The outer int still exists while control is in the inner block, even when its name is hidden. For the simple automatic ints here, lifetime begins after initialization and ends when their block is left. This is a bounded account of the current examples, not every C++ storage category.
Bytes potentially remaining somewhere do not make access after lifetime safe. We perform no such access and never read uninitialized values. The state table and block diagram are a language-level model, not a promise about physical stack placement.

records.title: Variables, blocks, and lifetime: a state journal
records.text:
A journal localizes a defect
Before running, record events such as stock created, beforeSale copied, stock changed, and block left. List existing objects, visible names, and values at each event. Compare printed checkpoints with the table. The first disagreement can expose a mistaken mental model rather than a compiler defect.
Distinguish repairing a program from correcting your prediction. Both are useful if the original hypothesis and actual output are retained. Preserve failed predictions in the record because they identify the confusion that was resolved.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
Sentinel: a value that terminates a sequence under its contract.
EOF: a state set after the end of input has been encountered.
Pre-test loop: the condition is checked before the body.
Post-test loop: the condition is checked after a mandatory initial body.
Progress: a change reducing the remaining work.
Finite stdin: a supplied buffer with a detectable end.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
Process an unknown number of items while distinguishing EOF, a sentinel, and malformed input.
Explain: Pre-test and post-test loops
Trace: Reading is a progress operation
Justify: Classify extraction failure
Implement and verify the lab against its exact contract.
Identify a common defect: An oversized final number can set both fail and eof. eof alone does not prove a token was valid.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
Pre-test and post-test loops
while(condition) tests before the body and can execute zero times. do {body} while(condition); tests after the body and executes at least once. The final semicolon is required for do while; after a regular while it usually creates an unintended empty body.
Choose according to the contract. A sequence should be processed only when another value exists, making while(std::cin>>x) natural. A mandatory initial action may use do while, but this never justifies using an unread x.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
Reading is a progress operation
In while(cin>>x), successful extraction supplies a new value and enters the body. Failure stops before x is used. Testing !cin.eof() before reading is wrong: eof reports an already encountered end rather than predicting the next extraction’s success.
When a condition contains only a flag, the body must update it or obtain new data. Ensure continue cannot skip the next progress operation. Even Nexus’s finite input cannot rescue a loop that has stopped consuming it.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
EOF, a sentinel, and a limit
EOF is the end of the supplied buffer; a sentinel such as 0 means stop under the task’s rules. The sentinel is consumed but usually excluded from the sum. State explicitly whether data after it is rejected or ignored.
A count limit bounds memory and time even for valid input. The lab permits at most 100 nonzero measurements with magnitude at most 1000, so the absolute sum cannot exceed 100000. Check the limit before changing the result.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
Classify extraction failure
After extraction stops, determine why. For the lab’s constrained short integers, an exhausted remainder is normal EOF and a letter is malformed input. With arbitrary tokens, fail and eof may both be set for an invalid or oversized number.
Preserve the distinction by first consuming allowed whitespace and checking EOF, then attempting extraction. If a token exists but extraction fails, reject it even if eof=true. Full line parsing and recovery are developed in the stream-state lesson.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
A stream invariant
Before each step, count is the number of accepted values, sum is their sum, and the buffer begins with unprocessed input. Validate the range before adding. On rejection, produce invalid rather than a partially successful answer.
Termination follows from consuming the remaining finite buffer on each successful read and explicitly handling failure. A sentinel stops earlier. Waiting for more input may be normal in an interactive terminal; Nexus supplies the whole stdin buffer before execution.

records.title: while and do while: finite streams and termination
records.text:
Choosing and checking the form
Use for for a known n and while for input until EOF or stop. do while suits repetition after one mandatory initial action. Do not simulate a live menu by waiting for input absent from the supplied buffer.
Test empty input, a sentinel alone, one value, normal EOF, a letter, and an oversized numeric token. Keep a count/sum trace. Next, extract the computation into a function so input handling and calculation can be tested separately.
